investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What does 'anechoic' mean on ultrasound and what causes it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Anechoic = completely black (no internal echoes), indicating simple fluid — e.g. a simple cyst, the full bladder, or ascites. Typically shows posterior acoustic enhancement behind it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Contrast acoustic shadowing with posterior acoustic enhancement.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Acoustic shadowing = dark band BEHIND a strongly reflective/attenuating structure (gallstone, calcification, gas). Posterior acoustic enhancement = bright band BEHIND a fluid-filled structure (cyst), because fluid barely attenuates sound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List the key advantages of abdominal ultrasound over CT.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• No ionising radiation (safe, repeatable, good in pregnancy/children)
  • cheap
  • portable/bedside
  • real-time and dynamic
  • and enables image-guided procedures (drains, biopsies).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What are the main limitations of abdominal ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• Highly operator-dependent
  • degraded by bowel gas and body habitus (obesity)
  • poor for the retroperitoneum and pancreas (CT superior)
  • small field of view.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Which organs/structures does a standard general abdominal US assess, and why fast the patient?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• Liver
  • gallbladder and biliary tree
  • pancreas (often gas-obscured)
  • spleen
  • kidneys
  • aorta
  • and free fluid.
Fasting distends the gallbladder, making stones and wall pathology easier to see.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the first-line imaging investigation for abnormal LFTs, hepatomegaly, RUQ pain, and HCC surveillance?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Liver ultrasound — cheap, quick, radiation-free; distinguishes diffuse from focal disease and cystic from solid, though it often cannot definitively characterise a solid lesion (needs CT/MRI).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Describe the ultrasound appearance of fatty liver (hepatic steatosis / NAFLD).
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: A bright/hyperechoic "bright liver" (brighter than the adjacent renal cortex) with posterior beam attenuation and loss of clarity of the intrahepatic vessels and diaphragm.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List the ultrasound features of cirrhosis and portal hypertension.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• Cirrhosis: coarse echotexture, nodular surface, small shrunken liver (or hypertrophied caudate/left lobe).
  • Portal hypertension: splenomegaly, ascites, dilated portal vein, recanalised umbilical vein.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: How do a simple cyst and a haemangioma appear on liver ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Simple cyst: anechoic, thin wall, posterior acoustic enhancement (benign). Haemangioma: well-defined, uniformly hyperechoic — the commonest benign solid liver lesion.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the HCC surveillance protocol in cirrhosis, and what does a new solid nodule mean?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: 6-monthly liver ultrasound (± AFP). A new solid nodule is possible HCC until proven otherwise → refer for contrast-enhanced CT/MRI characterisation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the first-line, gold-standard investigation for suspected gallstones and gallbladder disease?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Transabdominal ultrasound — cheap, radiation-free and highly sensitive for stones. Used to assess for stones, inflammation (cholecystitis) and biliary obstruction (CBD calibre).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Give the three classic ultrasound features of a gallstone.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• 1) A mobile, hyperechoic (bright) focus in the gallbladder lumen
  • 2) posterior acoustic shadowing behind it
  • 3) movement with gravity/position (rolls to the dependent part).
Mobility and shadowing distinguish it from a polyp.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List the ultrasound features of acute cholecystitis.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• Gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm)
  • pericholecystic fluid
  • gallbladder distension
  • a stone impacted in the neck/cystic duct
  • and a positive sonographic Murphy's sign (maximal tenderness under the probe over the gallbladder).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: A dilated common bile duct (>6–7 mm) on ultrasound suggests what, and what is the next step if a duct stone is suspected?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: It suggests biliary obstruction — choledocholithiasis (CBD stone), stricture or tumour. Ultrasound is insensitive for CBD stones themselves (bowel gas obscures the distal duct), so proceed to MRCP or endoscopic ultrasound (EUS).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is Charcot's triad and what condition does it indicate?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice — indicating ascending cholangitis, a biliary emergency requiring IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP). Adding hypotension and confusion gives Reynolds' pentad (septic shock).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Why is transabdominal ultrasound of the pancreas limited, and what is the main cross-sectional test instead?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: The pancreas is retroperitoneal and frequently obscured by overlying bowel gas, so US visualisation (especially of the tail) is poor. CT is the main cross-sectional test for pancreatic disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: In acute pancreatitis, what is the chief role of ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: To look for a gallstone aetiology (gallstones + dilated CBD → gallstone pancreatitis, the commonest cause alongside alcohol) rather than to assess the gland itself. Diagnosis is clinical + amylase/lipase, not imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is a pancreatic pseudocyst on ultrasound and when does it appear?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: A well-defined anechoic (fluid) collection, usually developing more than 4 weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What are the ultrasound features of chronic pancreatitis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• An atrophic gland
  • calcifications seen as echogenic foci with acoustic shadowing
  • and a dilated pancreatic duct.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the 'double-duct sign' and what does it suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Simultaneous dilatation of the common bile duct and pancreatic duct, typically from a hypoechoic mass in the pancreatic head — suggesting pancreatic adenocarcinoma. EUS and CT are superior for detection, staging and biopsy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the normal upper limit of splenic length on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: Approximately 12–13 cm bipolar (cranio-caudal) length; above this indicates splenomegaly.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: List five broad categories of causes of splenomegaly.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• Portal hypertension
  • haematological malignancy (lymphoma/leukaemia)
  • infection (EBV/infectious mononucleosis, malaria)
  • haemolytic anaemias
  • and infiltrative disorders (amyloid, sarcoid, storage diseases).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is the role of ultrasound (FAST) in blunt splenic trauma, and what determines management?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: FAST detects free intraperitoneal fluid (haemoperitoneum) and may show laceration/subcapsular haematoma. A haemodynamically UNSTABLE patient goes straight to theatre; a STABLE patient has CT as the definitive test to grade injury and guide conservative management.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Describe the classic ultrasound appearance of a splenic infarct and two associated conditions.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: A wedge-shaped, peripheral, hypoechoic lesion with its base at the capsule. Associations: septic emboli in infective endocarditis, and sickle cell disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: Why are patients with infectious mononucleosis advised to avoid contact sports?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: EBV causes an enlarged, fragile spleen at risk of atraumatic or minor-trauma rupture; contact sports are avoided (around 3–4 weeks / until recovery).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: What is Courvoisier’s law and why does it matter?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless jaundice is unlikely to be due to gallstones — it suggests obstruction by pancreatic or biliary malignancy (a chronically stone-diseased gallbladder is fibrosed and cannot distend). It flags a sinister cause needing urgent CT/EUS and an MDT.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.front: How does management differ between asymptomatic gallstones, biliary colic and acute cholecystitis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.back:
• Asymptomatic gallstones → no treatment.
  • Biliary colic (RUQ pain, NO fever/inflammatory signs, self-limiting) → analgesia + elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
  • Acute cholecystitis (stones + wall >3 mm + pericholecystic fluid + sonographic Murphy’s, fever/raised WCC) → admit, IV antibiotics and lap chole, ideally within 1 week / same admission.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What is the single most important question a renal ultrasound answers in acute kidney injury?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Is there obstruction (hydronephrosis)? Post-renal AKI is reversible if the collecting system is decompressed early, so US screens for a treatable cause before assuming pre-renal or intrinsic disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: How does hydronephrosis appear on ultrasound, and which pattern indicates obstructive AKI needing decompression?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Anechoic (black) branching fluid dilating the central renal sinus/pelvicalyceal system. Bilateral hydronephrosis — or unilateral in a single functioning kidney — with rising creatinine indicates post-renal AKI requiring nephrostomy or ureteric stent.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What are the ultrasound features of a renal stone, and why is CT KUB often preferred?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: A bright echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing. US detects renal-pelvis stones and hydronephrosis well, but CT KUB is more sensitive — especially for ureteric stones, which US frequently misses.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: List the ultrasound criteria for a simple (Bosniak I) renal cyst.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back:
• Anechoic contents
  • a thin imperceptible wall
  • and posterior acoustic enhancement (increased through-transmission).
It is benign and needs no follow-up; septa, calcification, wall thickening or solid components make it complex and require CT/MRI.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What ultrasound appearance characterises chronic kidney disease, and what does it imply?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Small, echogenic (bright) kidneys with cortical thinning and loss of corticomedullary differentiation. Bilateral small kidneys imply chronicity and irreversibility, steering away from aggressive investigation of reversible causes.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What aortic diameter defines an abdominal aortic aneurysm, and how is it measured?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Diameter ≥3 cm, measured outer-to-outer in the anteroposterior plane on ultrasound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Who does the NHS AAA Screening Programme invite, and what test is used?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Men in the year they turn 65 are offered a one-off abdominal ultrasound scan.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: State the ultrasound surveillance intervals for small and medium AAAs.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back:
• Small (3.0–4.4 cm): rescan yearly
  • Medium (4.5–5.4 cm): rescan 3-monthly.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: List the three triggers for vascular referral / consideration of elective AAA repair.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back:
• Diameter ≥5.5 cm
  • rapid expansion (>1 cm/year)
  • or symptomatic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Which imaging is used for a haemodynamically unstable patient with a suspected ruptured AAA?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: None that delays care — they go straight to theatre. Bedside POCUS may rapidly confirm the aneurysm; CT is reserved for stable patients.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: On ultrasound, how does intraperitoneal free fluid appear and where does it collect first?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: It appears anechoic (black) with no wall of its own, tracking around bowel loops. In a supine patient it pools first in the most dependent recesses — Morison's pouch (hepatorenal recess) is the most sensitive single site, along with the splenorenal recess and pelvis/pouch of Douglas.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What ultrasound features distinguish simple from complex ascites, and what does complex fluid suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back:
• Simple (transudative) fluid is uniformly anechoic
  • Complex fluid contains internal echoes, debris, septations or loculation — suggesting exudate, infection (e.g. TB), haemorrhage or malignancy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: How does the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) classify ascites?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back:
SAAG = serum albumin − ascitic albumin.
  • SAAG ≥11 g/L indicates portal hypertension (cirrhosis, heart failure — a transudate)
  • SAAG <11 g/L indicates a non-portal/exudative cause (malignancy, infection/TB, pancreatitis, nephrotic syndrome).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Why is ultrasound-guided paracentesis preferred, and what structures must be avoided?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back:
US marks a safe fluid pocket clear of hazards, making it safer than a blind tap. Avoid
  • bowel
  • the bladder
  • superficial/dilated vessels
  • and the inferior epigastric arteries running up the rectus sheath.
The classic entry is the left iliac fossa.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: How is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) diagnosed and when should you suspect it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Suspect SBP in any cirrhotic with fever, abdominal pain or unexplained encephalopathy. It is confirmed by an ascitic neutrophil (PMN) count ≥250/mm³ on diagnostic tap, and treated with empirical antibiotics. Any new ascites or decompensating cirrhotic warrants a diagnostic tap to exclude it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: Why is ultrasound the first-line imaging test for appendicitis in children, young women and pregnancy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: It avoids ionising radiation. In young women it also assesses gynaecological causes (ovary/adnexa) in the same study.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: List the core positive ultrasound features of acute appendicitis.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back:
• Blind-ending, non-compressible, aperistaltic tubular structure from the caecal pole
  • diameter >6 mm
  • target sign on cross-section
  • appendicolith (echogenic + shadowing)
  • periappendiceal fluid/echogenic inflamed fat
  • wall hyperaemia on Doppler.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What is the critical limitation of ultrasound in suspected appendicitis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: It is operator-dependent, and a non-visualised appendix does NOT exclude appendicitis — US can rule in but cannot rule out.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: If US is negative or equivocal but clinical suspicion of appendicitis persists, what next?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: Escalate: CT in adults, MRI in pregnancy, or observation / diagnostic laparoscopy — do not discharge.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What single test is mandatory in any woman of childbearing age with RIF pain, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: A pregnancy test, to exclude ectopic pregnancy before committing to a diagnosis or imaging pathway.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: A renal ultrasound shows a solid mass with no posterior acoustic enhancement. What is the pathway?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: A solid renal mass is a renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise (unlike a simple cyst, which is anechoic with posterior enhancement). Proceed to contrast CT to characterise and stage (chest/abdomen/pelvis) and refer to urology; the classic triad of haematuria, flank pain and a mass is late.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.front: What does free fluid on a FAST scan mean in an unstable trauma patient, and what is the action?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.back: It represents haemoperitoneum. In a haemodynamically unstable trauma patient a positive FAST mandates laparotomy — do not delay for CT. A stable patient can have CT to characterise the injury. FAST looks at the hepatorenal (Morison’s) and splenorenal recesses, the pelvis and the pericardium.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Why is a full bladder needed for a transabdominal pelvic ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: The distended bladder displaces gas-filled bowel loops out of the pelvis and acts as a fluid acoustic window, transmitting sound to allow the uterus, ovaries and adnexa to be seen.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Which probe and approach are used for TAUS?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: A low-frequency curvilinear probe applied suprapubically over the lower abdomen.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: List the key structures assessed on transabdominal pelvic ultrasound.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Uterus (size, position, fibroids, endometrial thickness)
  • ovaries and adnexa
  • free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
  • and the bladder itself

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Give two advantages and two limitations of TAUS versus transvaginal scanning.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
Advantages:
  • non-invasive
  • panoramic overview
  • good for large/extra-pelvic masses
  • suitable for children and virgins
Limitations:
  • lower resolution
  • degraded by obesity/bowel gas
  • useless with an empty bladder
  • retroverted uterus hard to see

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: In suspected ectopic pregnancy, what does a normal-looking TAUS mean?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: It does not exclude pathology. A technically limited or empty-bladder transabdominal scan is falsely reassuring, so proceed to transvaginal ultrasound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How does bladder preparation for transvaginal ultrasound differ from transabdominal, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: TVUS requires an EMPTY bladder (a full bladder pushes organs out of the probe's near field and degrades the close-up image), whereas transabdominal scanning needs a FULL bladder as an acoustic window.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: At what point is an intrauterine gestational sac expected on TVUS, and what does confirming one mean?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: From about 5 weeks / when serum hCG exceeds the discriminatory zone (~1500 IU/L). Confirming an intrauterine pregnancy makes ectopic very unlikely (heterotopic is rare, higher only with IVF).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What endometrial thickness on TVUS is reassuring vs concerning in postmenopausal bleeding, and what is the next step if thickened?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: 4 mm or less is reassuring; a thickened endometrium (>4 mm) requires hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy to exclude endometrial cancer.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Which TVUS features suggest a tubal ectopic pregnancy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: An adnexal mass separate from the ovary, an echogenic 'tubal ring', and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas — especially with an empty uterus and positive hCG.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: When is TVUS inappropriate, and what is the alternative?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• When the patient is not sexually active
  • cannot tolerate a speculum
  • declines
  • or in some cultural situations
Use transabdominal ultrasound (full bladder) instead. TVUS always needs consent and a chaperone.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How is endometrial thickness correctly measured on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Double-layer (both endometrial surfaces) at the widest point on the transvaginal SAGITTAL/midline view, excluding the hypoechoic myometrial halo and any intracavity fluid.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: In a woman with postmenopausal bleeding, what endometrial thickness is reassuring, and what is the cut-off for further investigation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: ≤4 mm is reassuring (endometrial cancer very unlikely). >4 mm requires hysteroscopy plus endometrial biopsy (pipelle) to exclude endometrial carcinoma.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do fibroids and adenomyosis differ on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Fibroid = focal, well-defined rounded hypoechoic myometrial mass (may shadow/calcify/degenerate)
  • Adenomyosis = diffusely enlarged 'globular' uterus, heterogeneous myometrium with cysts and a poorly defined/thickened junctional zone; no discrete mass

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What ultrasound features suggest an endometrial polyp, and what test helps delineate it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Focal echogenic thickening within the endometrial cavity with a single feeding vessel on Doppler. Saline infusion sonography (sonohysterography) distends the cavity to outline it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do you distinguish a bicornuate from a septate uterus, and why does it matter?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Bicornuate: the EXTERNAL fundal contour is split (fundal cleft/two horns)
  • Septate: external contour is intact/single with an internal septum
The distinction changes management (septum can be resected hysteroscopically).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What three ultrasound features define a simple (benign, usually functional) ovarian cyst?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Anechoic (fluid-filled)
  • thin smooth wall with no septations or solid components
  • and posterior acoustic enhancement
Usually a follicular or corpus luteal cyst — benign and typically resolves spontaneously.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do you distinguish an endometrioma from a dermoid on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Endometrioma ("chocolate cyst") = homogeneous low-level "ground-glass" echoes, no solid vascular nodule
  • Dermoid/mature teratoma = echogenic focus with fat and calcification and "tip of the iceberg" acoustic shadowing obscuring the deep wall

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What is the current ultrasound threshold for polycystic ovarian morphology, and does it diagnose PCOS?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: ≥20 follicles (2–9 mm) per ovary and/or ovarian volume >10 mL. Ultrasound alone does NOT diagnose PCOS — PCOS requires 2 of 3 Rotterdam criteria (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic morphology).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What ultrasound features suggest an ovarian malignancy, and what does RMI combine?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Solid components
  • thick (>3 mm) septations
  • papillary projections
  • bilaterality
  • ascites
  • and high Doppler flow
RMI = Ultrasound score × Menopausal status × CA-125; RMI >200 prompts gynae-oncology referral.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Why can ovarian torsion have preserved Doppler flow, and what does this mean clinically?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: The ovary has a dual blood supply (ovarian and uterine arteries), so arterial flow may persist despite torsion. A normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion — clinical suspicion mandates urgent laparoscopy to detorse and salvage the ovary.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Which ultrasound approach is first-line for early pregnancy assessment, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS). The probe sits closer to the pelvic organs, giving better resolution of early landmarks than transabdominal scanning.It is performed in the Early Pregnancy Assessment Unit (EPAU) alongside serum hCG.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: List the normal early ultrasound landmarks and their approximate gestational ages.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Intrauterine gestational sac ~4.5–5 weeks
  • yolk sac ~5.5 weeks
  • fetal pole with heartbeat ~6 weeks
The yolk sac is the first structure confirming a true intrauterine pregnancy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What is the discriminatory zone and how is it used?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: The serum hCG level (~>1500 IU/L) above which an intrauterine gestational sac should be visible on TVUS. If hCG is above this and the uterus is empty, ectopic pregnancy becomes much more likely.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: State the NICE/RCOG ultrasound criteria for a non-viable (miscarried) pregnancy.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Fetal pole with crown-rump length ≥7 mm and NO heartbeat
  • OR mean gestational sac diameter ≥25 mm with no fetal pole
If below these thresholds or uncertain, rescan in 7–14 days before diagnosing miscarriage.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What ultrasound features suggest an ectopic pregnancy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Empty uterus with positive pregnancy test (pregnancy of unknown location)
  • adnexal mass separate from the ovary
  • tubal 'ring/bagel' sign
  • free fluid in the pouch of Douglas (haemoperitoneum)
  • and a pseudogestational sac in the uterus
Serial hCG with a suboptimal rise supports the diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What is the ellipsoid formula for estimating bladder volume on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Volume (mL) ≈ height × width × depth × 0.52, using three orthogonal diameters (craniocaudal, transverse and anteroposterior) measured in cm.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What post-void residual (PVR) volume is considered normal, and what is acceptable in the elderly?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Normal PVR is <50 mL; up to ~100 mL is acceptable, particularly in elderly patients.Persistently raised values indicate incomplete emptying.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: Why must a post-void residual be scanned immediately after voiding?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Any delay allows urine to re-accumulate from the kidneys, falsely raising the residual and making emptying look worse than it is.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How do bladder stones and bladder tumours differ on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
• Stones are echogenic, mobile (shift with patient position) and cast an acoustic shadow
  • tumours are non-mobile wall-based soft-tissue masses that do not move

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: What complications suggest high-pressure chronic retention, and what must you watch for after catheterisation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Bilateral hydronephrosis and post-obstructive AKI (rising creatinine). After catheterising, monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte shifts.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: An empty uterus with a positive β-hCG and an adnexal mass suggests ectopic. What are the management options?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back:
Assume ectopic until proven otherwise and refer to EPAU/gynaecology. Options:
  • expectant (low/falling hCG, asymptomatic)
  • medical — methotrexate (unruptured, hCG below threshold, no fetal heartbeat, reliable follow-up)
  • or surgical — salpingectomy (ruptured/haemodynamically unstable, or failed medical)
Give anti-D to RhD-negative women having surgery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.front: How does tamoxifen affect the endometrium on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.back: Tamoxifen has a paradoxical oestrogenic effect on the endometrium — it causes thickening, subendometrial cysts and polyps, and raises endometrial-cancer risk. The endometrium often looks thick/cystic, so the 4 mm rule is less reliable; any postmenopausal bleeding on tamoxifen still needs hysteroscopy + biopsy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: In what gestational window is the UK routine dating scan offered?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Between 11+2 and 14+1 weeks of gestation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Which measurement dates a first-trimester pregnancy most accurately, and over what range?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Crown-rump length (CRL), reliable from roughly 8.5 to 14 weeks.Beyond ~14 weeks (CRL >~84 mm) it becomes unreliable and head circumference is used instead.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What ultrasound sign indicates a dichorionic twin pregnancy, and what indicates a monochorionic one?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
• Dichorionic = lambda / twin-peak sign (triangular placental wedge between the membranes)
  • Monochorionic = T-sign (membrane meets placenta at 90° with no wedge)

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Why is chorionicity best determined at the dating scan?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Chorionicity is most accurately assessed in the first trimester, and it determines risk: monochorionic (shared placenta) twins are at risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome and need increased surveillance.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: When there is a discrepancy between LMP-based dates and scan dates, which is used to set the EDD?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The scan (CRL) date supersedes LMP-based dating and sets the estimated due date, standardising the timing of later screening.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is nuchal translucency and when is it measured?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The ultrasound-measured anechoic fluid space at the back of the fetal neck, measured on a mid-sagittal image as part of the UK first-trimester combined screening test, offered between 11+2 and 14+1 weeks.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What are the three components of the combined test?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
• Maternal age
  • nuchal translucency
  • serum biochemistry (β-hCG and PAPP-A)
combined into a single numerical chance of trisomy 21, 18 and 13.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What biochemical pattern is typical of trisomy 21 on first-trimester screening?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Raised β-hCG and low PAPP-A.(NT is also typically increased.)

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is offered after a higher-chance result (commonly ≥1 in 150)?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The offer of NIPT (cell-free fetal DNA) as an intermediate non-invasive step, or definitive diagnostic testing: chorionic villus sampling (CVS, ~11–14 wks) or amniocentesis (from ~15 wks). Invasive tests carry ~0.5–1% miscarriage risk.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is the alternative if the NT/combined test window is missed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: The second-trimester quadruple test (14–20 weeks), which screens for trisomy 21 only using maternal serum (AFP, hCG, uE3, inhibin A).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: When is the NHS anomaly scan offered, and under which programme?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Between 18+0 and 20+6 weeks of gestation, under the Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme (FASP).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What are the 'lemon' and 'banana' signs and what do they indicate?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
Cranial signs of open spina bifida:
  • the 'lemon' sign is scalloping of the frontal skull bones
  • and the 'banana' sign is the curved cerebellum wrapped around the brainstem with an obliterated cisterna magna

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: How does exomphalos differ from gastroschisis on the anomaly scan?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
• Exomphalos: herniated abdominal contents covered by a membranous sac at the cord insertion, associated with aneuploidy
  • Gastroschisis: free-floating uncovered bowel loops, usually to the right of the cord, typically isolated

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What does the scan report about the placenta, and what follow-up may be triggered?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: It documents placental location; a low-lying placenta or suspected placenta praevia is flagged for a repeat scan at around 32–36 weeks.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is a 'soft marker' and give three examples.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
A minor ultrasound finding that is not an anomaly itself but may prompt reassessment of aneuploidy risk. Examples:
  • echogenic bowel
  • echogenic intracardiac focus
  • mild pyelectasis
  • choroid plexus cyst

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Which single biometry measurement is most sensitive for detecting fetal growth restriction?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Abdominal circumference (AC) — it reflects fetal liver glycogen and subcutaneous fat, so it falls early in placental insufficiency (asymmetric, head-sparing FGR).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: How is fetal growth restriction (FGR) defined on a growth scan?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: EFW or AC below the 10th centile, especially with a static or falling trajectory across serial scans. Placental insufficiency typically produces an asymmetric pattern (low AC, preserved HC).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What two non-biometry parameters are assessed alongside size to judge fetal wellbeing?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
• Liquor volume (amniotic fluid index / deepest pool — oligohydramnios suggests placental insufficiency)
  • and umbilical artery Doppler (raised resistance / absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates placental compromise)

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What defines macrosomia / large-for-gestational-age, and what is the main association and intrapartum risk?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: EFW above the 90th centile. Associated with maternal diabetes; the key intrapartum risk is shoulder dystocia.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Name three clinical indications for arranging a growth scan.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
Any of:
  • SFH small/large for dates or crossing centiles
  • reduced fetal movements
  • and maternal risk factors — hypertension/pre-eclampsia, diabetes, previous SGA baby or stillbirth, multiple pregnancy

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is the progressive umbilical artery Doppler sequence in worsening placental insufficiency?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Raised pulsatility index (PI) → absent end-diastolic flow (AEDF) → reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF). REDF is the most advanced arterial sign and indicates severe insufficiency with high stillbirth risk.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What does a falling MCA pulsatility index indicate, and what is the cerebroplacental ratio?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: A falling MCA PI reflects cerebral vasodilation — the brain-sparing effect of a hypoxic fetus redistributing blood to the brain. CPR = MCA PI ÷ UA PI; a low CPR flags redistribution and predicts adverse outcome.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Why is MCA peak systolic velocity (PSV) measured, and what threshold triggers action?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Raised MCA PSV detects fetal anaemia (e.g. rhesus/red-cell alloimmunisation, parvovirus B19) due to low viscosity and a high-output state. PSV >1.5 multiples of the median (MoM) is the trigger to arrange intrauterine transfusion.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What ductus venosus finding is a late, pre-terminal sign, and how is it used?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: An absent or reversed a-wave reflects myocardial decompensation and raised right atrial pressure. It is a late sign used to time delivery in very preterm fetal growth restriction.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What uterine artery Doppler pattern predicts pre-eclampsia and FGR?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Persistently high resistance with early diastolic "notching" reflects failed trophoblastic invasion of the spiral arteries and predicts pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What are the five components of the biophysical profile and the maximum score?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
• Fetal breathing movements
  • gross body movements
  • fetal tone
  • amniotic fluid volume
  • and a reactive CTG (non-stress test)
Each scored 2 or 0, maximum 10.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: How is a BPP score interpreted?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back:
• 8–10 = reassuring/normal
  • 6 = equivocal (repeat or deliver depending on gestation)
  • ≤4 = abnormal, strong evidence of fetal hypoxia, usually prompts delivery

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What defines a normal amniotic fluid component on BPP?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: A single deepest vertical pool of ≥2 cm. Less than 2 cm (oligohydramnios) reflects chronic placental insufficiency.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: Which biophysical activities are lost first and last in progressive fetal hypoxia?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: CTG reactivity and fetal breathing movements are lost first (most hypoxia-sensitive); fetal tone is lost last (most resistant), reflecting CNS centres of differing sensitivity.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: What is the modified biophysical profile?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: A shorter screening test using only two components: amniotic fluid volume plus a CTG (non-stress test).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: When preterm delivery is planned for a growth-restricted fetus, what two drugs are given for the baby?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Antenatal corticosteroids (e.g. betamethasone) for fetal lung maturity if <~34–36 weeks, and magnesium sulphate for fetal neuroprotection when delivery is planned/expected before ~30–32 weeks (reduces cerebral palsy). Deliver in a unit with the right neonatal level.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.front: A 20-week scan shows a low-lying placenta. What is the pathway and what does confirmed praevia mean for delivery?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.back: Rescan at 32–36 weeks (most migrate up). If placenta praevia persists (placenta over/reaching the internal os): antepartum-haemorrhage risk, avoid vaginal examination/intercourse, and plan an elective caesarean at ~37–38 weeks; admit and give steroids if bleeding.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the first-line imaging test for suspected DVT?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Compression ultrasound (CUS) with Doppler — cheap, portable, radiation-free, directly interrogating the proximal deep veins (common femoral, femoral, popliteal).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the single most important ultrasound sign of DVT?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Non-compressibility — a normal vein collapses completely under gentle probe pressure, whereas a vein containing thrombus does not compress.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Define proximal versus distal DVT.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Proximal (above-knee) = popliteal and femoral veins. Distal = calf veins. Proximal DVT carries the higher risk of PE.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: In the UK pathway, what does a two-level Wells score of ≥2 ("DVT likely") trigger?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours; if not available, give interim anticoagulation plus a D-dimer and scan within 24 hours.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What does a negative proximal US with a positive D-dimer prompt?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: A repeat proximal ultrasound in about 6–8 days, to catch a calf-vein thrombus that may have propagated proximally.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the primary spectral Doppler parameter used to grade internal carotid artery stenosis, and which way does it move?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Peak systolic velocity (PSV) in the ICA — velocity rises as the lumen narrows, so a higher PSV indicates a tighter stenosis. Supported by ICA/CCA PSV ratio and end-diastolic velocity (EDV).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which patients with carotid stenosis should be referred for carotid endarterectomy, and in what timeframe?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Symptomatic patients (recent TIA or non-disabling ischaemic stroke in the anterior circulation) with 50–99% NASCET stenosis — ideally operated within 2 weeks of symptom onset.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How is degree of carotid stenosis reported, and what is the main clinical threshold?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: As a percentage using NASCET criteria. ~PSV ≥125 cm/s corresponds to ≥50% stenosis — the threshold for considering surgery in symptomatic patients (≥70% carries the greatest benefit).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which carotid Doppler findings are generally NOT treated with endarterectomy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• Near-occlusion / string sign
  • 100% (complete) occlusion
  • and asymptomatic stenosis
— all managed medically with antiplatelet, statin, BP control and smoking cessation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What plaque features on B-mode matter, and which is highest risk for embolism?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• Calcified plaque is bright with acoustic shadowing
  • soft/echolucent plaque is dark and carries the highest embolic risk
  • ulcerated plaque has a surface crater.
Also assess intima-media thickness.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the normal spectral Doppler waveform of a healthy peripheral limb artery, and what are its three components?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
Triphasic:
  • (1) sharp systolic forward-flow upstroke
  • (2) brief early-diastolic flow reversal below baseline (elastic recoil against high peripheral resistance)
  • (3) small late-diastolic forward flow.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How does the arterial waveform change distal to a significant stenosis or occlusion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: It progressively damps: triphasic → biphasic (loss of reversal) → monophasic (low-velocity, rounded, continuous forward flow with slow upstroke). A monophasic damped signal means significant disease lies proximal to the probe.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What peak systolic velocity ratio across a stenosis indicates a haemodynamically significant (≥50%) narrowing?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: A velocity ratio >2:1 (PSV within the stenosis compared to the normal segment just proximal) indicates ≥50% diameter stenosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Give the ABPI value bands and their interpretation.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• 0.9–1.2 normal
  • 0.5–0.9 intermittent claudication
  • <0.5 critical limb ischaemia
  • >1.3 falsely elevated due to incompressible calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What are the 6 Ps of acute limb ischaemia and why do they matter?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• Pain
  • Pallor
  • Pulselessness
  • Paraesthesia
  • Perishingly cold
  • Paralysis.
It is a surgical emergency threatening the limb within hours — needs urgent revascularisation/embolectomy and heparin; do NOT delay for elaborate imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is renal artery Doppler used to screen for, and what is its role?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: It is the non-invasive first-line screening test for renal artery stenosis (RAS), assessing renal artery velocities, intrarenal waveforms, kidney size and resistive index. Anatomical confirmation is by CT or MR angiography.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: List the key clinical indications for renal artery Doppler.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• Resistant/refractory hypertension
  • hypertension in a young person (FMD) or with an epigastric/flank bruit
  • recurrent 'flash' pulmonary oedema
  • unexplained or asymmetric renal size
  • and a rise in creatinine after starting an ACEi/ARB (clue to bilateral RAS or RAS in a solitary kidney).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Contrast the two main causes of RAS.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• Atherosclerosis — older patients, ostial/proximal lesion, commonest cause
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia — younger women, mid-to-distal vessel, 'string of beads' on angiography, responds well to angioplasty.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What Doppler findings indicate significant renal artery stenosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• Raised peak systolic velocity at the stenosis (e.g. >180–200 cm/s)
  • elevated renal-aortic ratio (>3.5)
  • and a downstream intrarenal 'tardus-parvus' waveform (delayed slow systolic upstroke, low resistive index).
Also look for a small kidney.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How is RAS managed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Often medical: ACEi/ARB with renal-function monitoring plus cardiovascular risk reduction. Angioplasty ± stent is selective (FMD, flash pulmonary oedema, rapidly declining function); routine stenting of atherosclerotic RAS does not clearly improve outcomes.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the normal direction and character of portal vein flow on Doppler?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Hepatopetal (towards the liver), gently phasic, low velocity (~15–40 cm/s). The main portal vein measures up to ~13 mm.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which single Doppler finding is most specific for portal hypertension, and name three supporting signs.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
Reversed (hepatofugal) portal flow. Supporting signs:
  • dilated portal vein >13 mm
  • splenomegaly
  • ascites
  • recanalised umbilical vein
  • and porto-systemic collaterals/varices.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: How does tumour thrombus differ from bland thrombus in the portal vein on Doppler, and what does it suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Tumour thrombus shows arterial flow WITHIN the thrombus (bland thrombus is avascular). Arterial signal within a portal vein thrombus suggests underlying hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Give the classic Doppler and morphological features of Budd-Chiari syndrome.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
Hepatic vein outflow obstruction:
  • absent/reversed/turbulent hepatic vein flow
  • hepatic vein thrombosis or webs
  • caudate lobe hypertrophy (spared due to separate IVC drainage)
  • and ascites.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Why is hepatic artery patency critical to check after liver transplant?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Hepatic artery thrombosis is the feared early post-transplant complication. The transplanted biliary tree depends solely on arterial supply, so arterial occlusion threatens the graft with ischaemic biliary necrosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: On pre-operative vein mapping, what minimum vein diameter is generally wanted for a successful AVF?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: A patent, distensible, superficial vein of at least ~2–2.5 mm diameter (measured under a light tourniquet).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: State the 'rule of 6s' for AVF maturation.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: By about 6 weeks: access flow >600 mL/min, vein diameter >6 mm, and vein depth <6 mm from the skin — then it is ready to cannulate.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What is the preferred order of vascular access and of fistula site for haemodialysis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back:
• Access: AVF > AV graft > central venous catheter
  • Fistula: radiocephalic (Brescia–Cimino) first, then brachiocephalic, then brachiobasilic transposition.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: Which Doppler findings suggest a haemodynamically significant fistula stenosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Focally raised peak systolic velocity with a PSV ratio >2–3 across the lesion (typically juxta-anastomotic or outflow), plus reduced overall access flow.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What ultrasound/clinical picture indicates dialysis access steal syndrome?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Distal hand ischaemia (pain, pallor, cold, weak pulse) with retrograde arterial flow in the artery distal to the anastomosis — a threatened hand needs urgent vascular review.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: A compression ultrasound confirms a proximal DVT. What is the management?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Anticoagulate with a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban) first-line, for a minimum of 3 months. Duration depends on provoked (3 months) vs unprovoked/ongoing risk (consider longer); in unprovoked DVT consider investigating for occult malignancy and screen for PE if symptomatic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.front: What distinguishes critical limb ischaemia from claudication, and what is the action?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.back: Critical (chronic) limb ischaemia = rest pain (>2 weeks), arterial ulcers or gangrene, with an ABPI <0.5 (or ankle pressure <50 mmHg). It is limb-threatening → urgent vascular referral for revascularisation (angioplasty/bypass), not conservative management like claudication.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Name the four standard TTE acoustic windows.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Parasternal (long- and short-axis)
  • apical (4/5/2/3-chamber)
  • subcostal
  • and suprasternal.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Which TTE window is best for assessing a pericardial effusion and the IVC?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: The subcostal window.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How is pulmonary artery systolic pressure estimated on TTE?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: From the tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity (using the modified Bernoulli equation) plus the estimated right atrial pressure from the IVC.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What echo findings define cardiac tamponade?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: A large pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle, in a breathless, hypotensive patient — an emergency needing echo-guided pericardiocentesis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: When is TOE preferred over TTE?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: When TTE windows are poor — obesity, COPD, ventilated patients — or when detailed views are needed (e.g. endocarditis vegetations, left atrial appendage thrombus, prosthetic valves).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Why does TOE give superior resolution of posterior cardiac structures compared with TTE?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: The probe sits in the oesophagus, directly behind the left atrium, with no lung or chest wall in the way and closer to posterior structures — allowing higher-frequency, higher-resolution imaging of the LA, LA appendage, mitral valve, prosthetic valves, aorta and interatrial septum.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Which structure, essentially invisible on TTE, makes TOE mandatory before cardioversion or appendage occlusion in AF?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: The left atrial appendage — TOE is used to detect (or exclude) LA appendage thrombus, which TTE cannot image well.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Why is TOE preferred over TTE in suspected infective endocarditis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: It is far more sensitive for vegetations, valve abscess and prosthetic-valve involvement, because prosthetic shadowing is bypassed and posterior detail is much clearer.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What preparation and risks make TOE a 'semi-invasive' test?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Needs consent, fasting, throat local anaesthetic and sedation; risks include oesophageal perforation and aspiration. Contraindicated in oesophageal stricture/varices/recent oesophageal surgery and unstable c-spine.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: List key indications for TOE.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Infective endocarditis
  • embolic source / pre-cardioversion LA appendage thrombus in AF
  • detailed mitral valve assessment before repair
  • prosthetic valve dysfunction
  • aortic dissection (especially unstable/intra-op)
  • PFO/ASD and shunts (bubble study)
  • and intra-operative monitoring in cardiac surgery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What defines a positive stress echo for inducible ischaemia?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: A myocardial segment that contracts normally at rest develops a NEW or WORSENING regional wall motion abnormality (hypokinesia/akinesia) during stress.The affected territory localises the culprit stenosed coronary artery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How does dobutamine stress the heart, and how does a vasodilator differ?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Dobutamine increases contractility and heart rate, raising myocardial oxygen demand to provoke ischaemia. A vasodilator (e.g. adenosine/dipyridamole) instead induces coronary steal, diverting flow away from segments supplied by stenosed vessels.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What is the biphasic response and what does it indicate?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: On low-dose dobutamine, a dysfunctional segment first IMPROVES contraction (low dose) then WORSENS at higher dose. This biphasic pattern indicates VIABLE / hibernating myocardium that may recover function after revascularisation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How does stress echo assess low-flow low-gradient aortic stenosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Dobutamine augments stroke volume and flow across the valve, differentiating TRUE severe AS (gradient rises, small valve area persists) from PSEUDO-severe AS (valve area increases as flow improves — the low gradient was due to poor LV function).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Name key contraindications/cautions for stress echo.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Acute coronary syndrome
  • severe uncontrolled hypertension
  • significant arrhythmia
  • and severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (especially for exercise).
Resuscitation facilities must be immediately available.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: In a normal agitated saline bubble study, why do no bubbles reach the left heart?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: The large saline bubbles opacify the right atrium and right ventricle, then are completely filtered by the pulmonary capillary bed and never cross to the left side.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Bubbles appear in the left heart within 3–5 beats of injection — what does this indicate, versus bubbles appearing after ~5 beats?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Early (3–5 beats) = intracardiac right-to-left shunt (PFO or ASD).
  • Late (>5 beats) = intrapulmonary shunt, e.g. a pulmonary AVM.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Why is a Valsalva manoeuvre or cough performed during a bubble study?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: It transiently raises right atrial pressure above left atrial pressure, opening the flap-valve PFO to unmask a right-to-left shunt that may be absent at rest.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What is the key clinical indication for an agitated saline bubble study?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Work-up of cryptogenic / young stroke, searching for a PFO that could allow paradoxical embolism.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How do commercial microbubble contrast agents differ from agitated saline, and what are they used for?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
They are small, shelled and stable enough to cross the lungs into the LV. Used for
  • LV cavity opacification to improve EF assessment
  • detect apical thrombus or apical HCM
  • and for myocardial perfusion imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How does FoCUS differ from a formal transthoracic echo (TTE)?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: FoCUS is a goal-directed, qualitative, rapid bedside scan done by trained clinicians to answer specific binary questions, integrated with the clinical picture. TTE is comprehensive and quantitative, performed by an accredited sonographer. FoCUS is not a substitute for TTE.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What are the core questions FoCUS is used to answer?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• (1) Pericardial effusion/tamponade?
  • (2) Grossly good or poor LV function (eyeball EF)?
  • (3) Dilated/strained RV suggesting massive PE?
  • (4) Volume status via IVC size and collapsibility?
  • (5) Any gross valve or obvious structural abnormality?

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Which view is the workhorse during cardiac arrest, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: The subcostal 4-chamber view — it gives effusion and gross function information and can be obtained in the pulse-check pause without interrupting chest compressions.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Which reversible causes of arrest (4 Hs / 4 Ts) can FoCUS help identify?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Tamponade (effusion + compressed heart)
  • massive PE (dilated strained RV)
  • hypovolaemia (empty hyperdynamic LV, flat IVC)
  • and — with lung ultrasound — tension pneumothorax (absent lung sliding).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What does the IVC tell you on a focused echo?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: IVC diameter and inspiratory collapsibility estimate volume status / right atrial pressure and fluid responsiveness — a small, collapsing IVC suggests hypovolaemia/fluid responsiveness; a large, non-collapsing IVC suggests high filling pressures.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What are the echocardiographic ejection-fraction categories of heart failure?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Normal EF >50%.
  • HFrEF = EF ≤40% (reduced).
  • HFmrEF = EF 41–49% (mildly reduced).
  • HFpEF = EF ≥50% with evidence of diastolic dysfunction (raised E/e′, enlarged LA).
HFrEF triggers the four pillars of guideline HF therapy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: TOE before cardioversion shows a left-atrial-appendage thrombus. What do you do?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Do NOT cardiovert (risk of embolic stroke). Anticoagulate for ~3–4 weeks and re-image with TOE; cardiovert only once the thrombus has resolved.TOE is used precisely because it images the LA appendage that TTE cannot see well.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What is the formula for ejection fraction, and what is the normal value?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV. Normal is ≥50%.It is the key measure of LV systolic function and is measured most accurately by Simpson's biplane method.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Define HFrEF, HFmrEF and HFpEF by ejection fraction.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• HFrEF = heart failure with reduced EF (≤40%)
  • HFmrEF = mildly reduced EF (41–49%)
  • HFpEF = preserved EF (≥50%) with symptoms/signs, raised natriuretic peptides and structural/functional echo abnormality.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How is Simpson's biplane method performed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: The LV endocardial border is traced at end-diastole and end-systole in the apical 4-chamber and apical 2-chamber views; the LV cavity is modelled as a stack of discs to calculate EDV, ESV and hence EF.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What does the E/e′ ratio represent, and what value suggests raised filling pressures?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: E/e′ combines mitral inflow early velocity (E, pulsed Doppler) with mitral annular early velocity (e′, tissue Doppler) as a surrogate for LV filling pressure. E/e′ >14 suggests elevated LV filling / left atrial pressures.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: List the three grades of diastolic dysfunction in order of severity.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• (1) Impaired relaxation (E/A <0.8, normal pressures)
  • (2) Pseudonormal (E/A normalises but E/e′ and LA size raised)
  • (3) Restrictive filling (E/A >2, high E/e′, severe LA enlargement) — advanced disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What is the modified Bernoulli equation and what does it convert?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: ΔP = 4v². It converts the peak blood velocity (v, in m/s) measured by continuous-wave Doppler across a valve into a pressure gradient (ΔP, in mmHg). E.g. a 4 m/s aortic jet gives a peak gradient of 64 mmHg.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Give the three echo criteria for severe aortic stenosis.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Peak velocity >4 m/s
  • mean gradient >40 mmHg
  • and aortic valve area <1.0 cm² (or indexed <0.6 cm²/m²).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How is severe aortic regurgitation identified on echo?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Wide jet/vena contracta relative to the LVOT
  • a short pressure half-time (rapid aorta-LV pressure equalisation)
  • and holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending/abdominal aorta.
Also assess LV dilatation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How does echo distinguish primary from secondary mitral regurgitation, and how is severity quantified?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• Primary = intrinsic valve disease (prolapse, flail leaflet, endocarditis)
  • secondary/functional = normal valve tethered by a dilated/dysfunctional LV.
Severity is quantified with jet area, vena contracta, and the PISA method giving EROA and regurgitant volume.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What are the echo hallmarks of mitral stenosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
Almost always rheumatic.
  • "Hockey-stick" diastolic doming of the thickened anterior leaflet
  • valve area by planimetry or pressure half-time (severe <1.5 cm²)
  • left atrial enlargement
  • thrombus/spontaneous echo contrast
  • and associated AF.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: On parasternal long-axis, how do you distinguish a pericardial from a pleural effusion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
By its relationship to the descending thoracic aorta:
  • pericardial fluid tracks ANTERIOR to the aorta
  • pleural fluid tracks POSTERIOR to it.
Pericardial effusion is also circumferential; the pericardial fat pad is anterior-only and speckled.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Which echo sign of tamponade is the earliest/most sensitive, and which is the most specific?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Right ATRIAL systolic collapse (free-wall inversion, when RA pressure is lowest) is the earliest/most sensitive sign. Right VENTRICULAR diastolic collapse is the most specific. With a dilated non-collapsing IVC and a swinging heart, these indicate tamponade → urgent pericardiocentesis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What does a dilated, non-collapsing (plethoric) IVC indicate in suspected tamponade?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: A raised right atrial pressure — a near-universal finding in tamponade. IVC that fails to collapse >50% on inspiration supports the diagnosis; a normally collapsing IVC makes tamponade unlikely.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Why can a small effusion tamponade while a large one may not?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Speed of accumulation. The pericardium is acutely non-compliant but stretches over time. Rapid bleeds (post-MI free-wall rupture, trauma, aortic dissection, post-procedure) tamponade at small volumes; chronic effusions can hold 1–2 L while the pericardium accommodates.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What is the definitive management of cardiac tamponade, and what should you avoid?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis (or surgical drainage/pericardial window). Support preload with IV fluids; AVOID over-diuresis, as the tamponading heart is preload-dependent.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What does global longitudinal strain (GLS) measure, and what technique is used?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: GLS measures myocardial deformation — the percentage change in length (shortening) of segments from base to apex during systole — using speckle-tracking echocardiography, which follows the natural acoustic speckle pattern of the myocardium frame-by-frame.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Why are strain values negative, and what does a less negative GLS mean?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Values are negative because the muscle shortens. Normal GLS is about −18% to −20% or more negative. A LESS negative value (e.g. −12%) means WORSE function — 'more negative = better'.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: Why can GLS detect systolic dysfunction before ejection fraction falls?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: The longitudinal subendocardial fibres are the most vulnerable and fail first; GLS interrogates exactly these fibres. EF is dominated by circumferential/radial function and stays normal until later, so GLS drops earlier and detects subclinical dysfunction.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: How is GLS used in cardio-oncology, and what threshold triggers action?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Serial GLS monitoring during cardiotoxic chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab). A relative fall in GLS >15% from baseline predicts later cardiotoxicity and prompts cardioprotection before EF drops — signalling subclinical CTRCD.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What bull's-eye GLS pattern is characteristic of cardiac amyloidosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: 'Apical sparing' — the 'cherry on top' pattern: reduced strain in the basal and mid segments with relatively preserved (better) strain at the apex on the polar bull's-eye map.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: What are the four pillars of guideline therapy for HFrEF?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back:
• (1) ARNI (sacubitril-valsartan) or an ACE inhibitor/ARB
  • (2) a beta-blocker
  • (3) a mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone)
  • (4) an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin).
Add a loop diuretic for congestion; consider an ICD/CRT if EF ≤35% despite optimal therapy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.front: When is severe aortic stenosis treated, and how?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.back: Intervene when it is symptomatic (angina, syncope, breathlessness) or asymptomatic with LV EF <50%. Treatment is aortic valve replacement — surgical AVR (younger/low-risk) or TAVI (older/higher surgical risk). Vasodilators/nitrates are used with caution in severe AS.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Which imaging is first-line for a thyroid nodule or goitre?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: High-resolution neck ultrasound with a high-frequency linear probe, alongside TFTs. It characterises the gland, focal nodules and cervical nodes and guides FNA.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: List the classic suspicious (malignant) ultrasound features of a thyroid nodule.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Solid and hypoechoic
  • microcalcifications (punctate bright foci)
  • irregular/lobulated margins
  • taller-than-wide shape (AP > transverse)
  • increased intranodular vascularity
  • abnormal cervical lymph nodes.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: What does the BTA U-classification signify and which scores need FNA?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• U1 normal
  • U2 benign
  • U3 indeterminate
  • U4 suspicious
  • U5 malignant.
U3–U5 require ultrasound-guided FNA cytology (reported with the Thy classification).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Contrast the ultrasound appearances of Graves' disease and Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Graves': diffusely enlarged, markedly hypervascular gland ('thyroid inferno' on Doppler)
  • Hashimoto's: heterogeneous, hypoechoic, coarse/micronodular texture.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Why can't thyroid ultrasound tell you if a nodule is 'hot' or toxic?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Ultrasound assesses structure, not function. Thyroid function is measured by TFTs, and a hot/toxic nodule is defined by increased uptake on radionuclide (technetium/iodine) scanning, not on ultrasound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Which ultrasound features characterise a benign (reactive) cervical lymph node?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Oval shape with long-to-short axis ratio >2
  • a preserved echogenic fatty hilum
  • a smooth thin cortex
  • and central hilar vascularity on Doppler.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: List the ultrasound features that make a cervical node suspicious for malignancy/metastasis.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Round shape (ratio <2)
  • loss of the fatty hilum
  • cortical thickening/eccentric cortex
  • peripheral/chaotic capsular vascularity
  • cystic/necrotic change
  • microcalcification (papillary thyroid mets) and matting.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Why can a lymphomatous node be misleading on ultrasound, and what biopsy is required?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Nodes are often multiple, rounded and hypoechoic ('pseudocystic') but a hilar-type vascularity may persist, mimicking benign flow. FNA is usually insufficient to subtype lymphoma, so a core or excision biopsy is required.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: What are the classic ultrasound features of tuberculous cervical nodes?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Matted, necrotic nodes that may form a cold abscess or a discharging sinus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: How should a hard, fixed, painless, enlarging cervical node in an older adult be managed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Treat as head & neck squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise: 2-week-wait ENT referral for US-guided FNA/core biopsy and panendoscopy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Colour Doppler findings of testicular torsion on scrotal ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Reduced or absent intratesticular colour Doppler flow
  • an enlarged hypoechoic (oedematous) testis
  • and a "whirlpool sign" of the twisted spermatic cord.
But torsion is a clinical diagnosis — do not delay exploration for a classic story; the salvage window is ~6 hours.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: How does epididymo-orchitis differ from torsion on Doppler?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: It shows the opposite pattern: INCREASED colour flow in a hyperaemic, enlarged epididymis/testis, often with a reactive hydrocele. Torsion shows reduced/absent flow. Doppler flow is the key discriminator between these two.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: A solid intratesticular mass on ultrasound — diagnosis and management?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
Germ cell tumour (seminoma or non-seminomatous) until proven otherwise.
  • Urgent urology
  • tumour markers AFP/β-hCG/LDH
  • staging CT
  • and radical INGUINAL orchidectomy.
Never perform a trans-scrotal biopsy (risks tumour seeding).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Ultrasound features of a varicocele and when it needs further imaging?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: "Bag of worms" dilated pampiniform plexus veins >2–3 mm that augment on Valsalva, usually left-sided. A new right-sided or non-reducing varicocele warrants renal/retroperitoneal imaging to exclude an obstructing mass.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Which acute scrotal condition after trauma needs surgery, and its US sign?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Testicular rupture — a breach of the tunica albuginea, seen as a heterogeneous testis with contour disruption. It requires surgical exploration and repair.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: What are the three components of breast triple assessment?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Clinical examination
  • imaging (ultrasound and/or mammography)
  • tissue biopsy (core biopsy ± FNA).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Why is ultrasound first-line imaging in women under ~40?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Younger women have denser fibroglandular breast tissue that limits mammographic sensitivity; US avoids ionising radiation and characterises focal lesions well. In older women it complements mammography.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: List the ultrasound features suggesting a benign lesion.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Oval shape
  • wider-than-tall (parallel to skin)
  • well-circumscribed
  • smooth thin capsule
  • hypo/isoechoic
  • few internal echoes.
E.g. fibroadenoma and simple cysts (anechoic, thin wall, posterior enhancement).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: List the ultrasound features suggesting malignancy.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Irregular/spiculated margins
  • taller-than-wide (vertical growth)
  • hypoechoic
  • posterior acoustic shadowing
  • internal microcalcifications
  • architectural distortion
  • ductal extension
  • and abnormal axillary nodes (cortical thickening, loss of fatty hilum).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: What scoring systems are used to report breast ultrasound findings?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: U1–U5 (U1 normal, U5 highly suspicious of malignancy) or BI-RADS. Suspicious (U4/U5) lesions proceed to US-guided core biopsy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Which salivary gland most commonly harbours stones, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: The submandibular gland (Wharton's duct) — its secretions are more mucinous/viscous and it drains against gravity, so ~80% of sialoliths occur here.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Ultrasound triad of a salivary stone?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: An echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing, usually with proximal ductal dilatation behind the obstruction. Presents with mealtime pain/swelling.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Ultrasound appearance of acute sialadenitis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: A diffusely enlarged, hypoechoic, hypervascular gland (increased Doppler flow). A complex fluid collection indicates abscess formation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Name the two commonest benign parotid tumours and their US features.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Pleomorphic adenoma (commonest; well-defined lobulated hypoechoic superficial-lobe mass)
  • and Warthin's tumour (cystic, often bilateral, older male smokers).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: What US pattern suggests Sjögren's syndrome and what is the key associated risk?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Multiple small hypo-/anechoic areas giving a heterogeneous 'leopard-skin'/honeycomb gland, often bilateral. Associated with an increased risk of lymphoma.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: What is the first-line imaging modality for a palpable soft-tissue / subcutaneous lump, and what three-way triage does it provide?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
Ultrasound. It sorts lumps into
  • obviously benign (reassure, no follow-up)
  • indeterminate
  • or suspicious/red-flag (→ MRI + sarcoma MDT + core biopsy).
No radiation, real-time compressibility, and colour Doppler for vascularity.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: Describe the classic ultrasound appearance of a lipoma.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Well-defined
  • soft/compressible
  • elongated and lying parallel to the skin
  • iso- to hyperechoic relative to fat
  • with thin internal echogenic striations and minimal/no vascularity.
