Classic features need no follow-up.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: How does an abscess appear on ultrasound and Doppler?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: A complex collection with internal debris, an avascular centre (no internal Doppler flow), but a hyperaemic surrounding rim. May be aspirated or drained.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: List the clinical red-flag features of a soft-tissue lump that suggest sarcoma.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back:
• Size >5 cm
  • deep to fascia
  • hard/fixed
  • rapidly enlarging
  • painful
  • or recurrence after previous excision.
On US: irregular margins, heterogeneous echotexture, internal vascularity.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: What is the correct management of a lump with red-flag/sarcoma features, and why not just excise it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: Refer to a specialist sarcoma centre for MRI and image-guided core biopsy BEFORE any excision. Unplanned ("whoops") excision contaminates tissue planes, mandates wider re-excision, and worsens outcomes.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.front: How is a pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid managed, and why not simply enucleate it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.back: By superficial parotidectomy (with facial-nerve preservation), NOT enucleation — the tumour has microscopic capsular pseudopods, so enucleation leaves tumour behind and recurs, and shelling it out risks facial-nerve injury. Left untreated it can undergo malignant transformation. (Contrast: Warthin’s tumour is benign, often just observed.)

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Which rotator cuff tendon is most commonly injured, and what is the normal ultrasound appearance of a cuff tendon?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: Supraspinatus. A normal tendon is a uniform, fibrillar, moderately echogenic band that hugs the humeral head and inserts on the greater tuberosity.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: List the ultrasound features of a FULL-thickness rotator cuff tear.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
A defect spanning the whole tendon:
  • non-visualisation/retraction of the tendon
  • fluid tracking into the gap
  • and a bare/"naked" greater tuberosity with the deltoid falling onto the humeral head.
(Partial-thickness = focal hypoechoic/anechoic defect NOT crossing the full width.)

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: How is calcific tendinitis distinguished from tendinopathy on shoulder ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• Calcific tendinitis = a bright echogenic calcific deposit ± posterior acoustic shadowing within supraspinatus (acutely very painful)
  • Tendinopathy = a thickened, heterogeneous, hypoechoic tendon with loss of fibrillar pattern but NO discrete tear or calcification.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Why is ultrasound the first-line test for suspected rotator cuff pathology?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• It is dynamic (scan during movement to show impingement/bunching under the acromion)
  • cheap
  • radiation-free
  • allows direct side-to-side comparison
  • and can guide a targeted injection.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: When should MRI be used instead of/after ultrasound for the shoulder?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• For surgical planning
  • deep or large/massive tears
  • assessing muscle atrophy/fatty infiltration
  • and for labral and bony detail that ultrasound cannot resolve.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What is the normal long-axis ultrasound appearance of a tendon?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: An ordered fibrillar echotexture — tightly packed parallel hyperechoic (bright) lines running along the tendon. Loss of this pattern suggests pathology.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What is anisotropy and why does it matter in tendon ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: An artefact where a tendon falsely appears hypoechoic (dark) when the probe beam is not perpendicular to the fibres. It disappears on angling the probe to 90 degrees, distinguishing it from true tendinopathy or tear — the classic pitfall.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: How does ultrasound distinguish a partial from a complete tendon tear?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• Partial tear = focal fibre discontinuity interrupting only some fibres
  • Complete/full-thickness tear = discontinuity across the whole tendon with a gap, retracted refractile ends, and separation of the ends on dynamic scanning.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What are the ultrasound features of tendinopathy?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: Thickened, hypoechoic tendon with loss of the normal fibrillar pattern and neovascularity (abnormal blood flow) on colour/power Doppler. Examples: Achilles, patellar, common extensor origin (tennis elbow).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What ultrasound findings define tenosynovitis, and give a classic example?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: Fluid and/or thickening within the tendon SHEATH with hyperaemia on Doppler, often with a relatively normal tendon core. Classic example: De Quervain's tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment at the radial wrist.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Why is ultrasound preferred over clinical exam or plain film for detecting a joint effusion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: US is more sensitive than palpation or radiographs — it detects effusions too small to feel or see on film, is radiation-free, and can guide aspiration.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Ultrasound appearance of a SIMPLE joint effusion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: Anechoic (uniformly black) and compressible/displaceable — the fluid shifts when you press with the probe. Suggests transudate/simple fluid (e.g. OA, reactive).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What does a COMPLEX effusion (internal echoes, debris, septations) suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: Cells or protein within the fluid — think haemarthrosis (blood: trauma, anticoagulation), pus (septic arthritis) or inflammatory debris. Aspirate to characterise.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: How do you distinguish active synovitis from an effusion on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• Synovitis is hypoechoic thickened synovium, NON-compressible, with increased power Doppler flow (active inflammation)
  • An effusion is compressible with no Doppler flow inside it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Ultrasound crystal-disease clues: gout vs pseudogout?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• Gout: double contour sign — hyperechoic urate line ON TOP of the cartilage surface (plus tophi/aggregates)
  • Pseudogout (CPPD): hyperechoic deposits WITHIN the cartilage itself (chondrocalcinosis).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Why are ultrasound-guided injections more accurate than blind/landmark injections?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: US shows the needle tip and target in real time, and lets you watch the anechoic injectate distribute into the correct compartment — confirming intra-articular/intra-bursal placement rather than relying on surface landmarks and feel. Especially valuable for deep or small targets.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Distinguish in-plane from out-of-plane needle technique.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• In-plane: needle runs along the probe's long axis, so the whole shaft and tip are seen as a continuous bright line (preferred)
  • Out-of-plane: needle crosses the beam and is seen only as a single bright dot, so true tip depth can be lost.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: How do you confirm correct placement during an US-guided injection?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: Watch the anechoic injectate distribute in real time — it should fill the intended compartment (distend a bursa, flow along a tendon sheath). If fluid pools within tendon fibres and fails to spread, you are intratendinous and must reposition.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: List the main advantages of US-guided injection over blind and over fluoroscopic guidance.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• vs blind: accuracy, confirmed intra-articular/intra-bursal placement, real-time avoidance of vessels and nerves.
  • vs fluoroscopy: no ionising radiation.
US is portable and dynamic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What are the key complications/cautions of corticosteroid injection?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• Infection (needs aseptic technique)
  • steroid flare
  • skin depigmentation and fat atrophy at the site
  • and tendon rupture if injected intratendinously.
Check anticoagulation and consent. Never inject into infected tissue or into a tendon.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: On groin ultrasound, how do you distinguish an indirect from a direct inguinal hernia?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
Locate the inferior epigastric vessels with Doppler.
  • An INDIRECT hernia sac arises LATERAL to the vessels and enters the deep ring/inguinal canal
  • a DIRECT hernia pushes through the posterior wall MEDIAL to the vessels.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What is the key strength of ultrasound over other imaging for a suspected hernia?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: It is a dynamic, real-time test. Scanning during a Valsalva manoeuvre, cough, or standing shows the sac and contents bulging through the defect and reducing on relaxation — allowing detection of an occult (impalpable) hernia.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: How is a femoral hernia located on ultrasound, and why does it matter?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• It lies BELOW the inguinal ligament
  • medial to the femoral vein
  • and below/lateral to the pubic tubercle.
Its narrow rigid neck makes strangulation much more likely; it is commoner in women.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: How does ultrasound differentiate a saphena varix from a hernia?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: A saphena varix is a dilatation at the sapheno-femoral junction that COLLAPSES when the patient lies flat, refills on standing/Valsalva, and shows venous flow on colour Doppler — unlike a hernia sac containing bowel or fat.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: Which ultrasound features suggest a strangulated hernia requiring emergency surgery?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back:
• An irreducible, tender sac
  • ABSENT Doppler flow in the contained bowel wall
  • wall thickening
  • surrounding free fluid
  • and dilated obstructed proximal bowel loops
— indicating ischaemia and needing urgent surgical referral.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: What is a Baker’s cyst and why does it matter on a leg ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: A popliteal (Baker’s) cyst is fluid in the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa that communicates with the knee joint (often with an effusion/OA). A ruptured Baker’s cyst causes acute calf pain and swelling and classically mimics a DVT — ultrasound distinguishes the two.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.front: How is a suspected Achilles tendon rupture diagnosed and initially managed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.back: It is a clinical diagnosis — a palpable gap and a positive Simmonds/Thompson calf-squeeze test (no plantarflexion); US/MRI confirm and size the gap. Initially immobilise in equinus (plantarflexion) and refer to orthopaedics; conservative functional bracing and surgery have comparable re-rupture rates.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What does FAST stand for and what single question does it answer?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma — a rapid bedside scan asking a binary question: is there FREE FLUID (assumed to be blood) in the peritoneum or pericardium?

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Name the four standard FAST views.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back:
• (1) RUQ/hepatorenal = Morison's pouch
  • (2) LUQ/perisplenic (splenorenal)
  • (3) Pelvis (rectovesical / pouch of Douglas)
  • (4) Subxiphoid pericardial view.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Which FAST view is most sensitive in a supine patient and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: The RUQ view of Morison's pouch (hepatorenal recess) — it is the most dependent intraperitoneal space when the patient lies supine, so free fluid pools there first.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What does eFAST add, and what signs indicate a pneumothorax?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back:
eFAST adds bilateral thoracic views. Pneumothorax =
  • loss of lung sliding
  • absent comet-tails
  • "barcode/stratosphere sign" on M-mode
  • and the lung point (highly specific).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: How does management differ for a positive FAST in an unstable vs stable patient?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Positive + unstable → straight to laparotomy (no CT delay). Positive + stable → CT to characterise/grade the injury. A negative FAST does not exclude injury.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What three ultrasound findings confirm normal, aerated lung?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back:
• Lung sliding ("ants marching" shimmer of the pleura with respiration)
  • A-lines (regularly spaced horizontal reverberation artefacts parallel to the pleura)
  • and the seashore sign on M-mode.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Which lung ultrasound sign is pathognomonic for pneumothorax, and what is it?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: The lung point — the transition zone where sliding (normal) lung meets non-sliding (pneumothorax) lung as the patient breathes. It confirms pneumothorax and marks its edge.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What are B-lines and what does finding ≥3 in one field indicate?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: B-lines are vertical hyperechoic "comet-tail" artefacts running from the pleura to the bottom of the screen, moving with sliding and erasing A-lines. ≥3 per field = interstitial syndrome / "wet lung"; bilateral diffuse B-lines suggest cardiogenic pulmonary oedema or ARDS.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: On M-mode, how do normal lung and pneumothorax differ?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Normal lung gives the seashore sign (horizontal "waves" above the pleura, granular "sandy beach" below from moving lung). Pneumothorax gives the barcode / stratosphere sign (uniform horizontal lines throughout because there is no movement below the pleura).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What ultrasound features suggest consolidation versus a pleural effusion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Consolidation (pneumonia): tissue-like "hepatisation" of lung with dynamic air bronchograms. Pleural effusion: an anechoic collection above the diaphragm with the spine sign, quad sign and floating "jellyfish" collapsed lung; US guides thoracocentesis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Where and how is the IVC measured on point-of-care ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Subcostal long-axis view, measuring the diameter ~2 cm distal to the hepatic vein/right atrial junction, perpendicular to the vessel wall. Assess both maximum diameter and respiratory variation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What does a small (<1–1.5 cm), highly collapsing (>50%) IVC suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Low right atrial pressure, hypovolaemia, and a patient who is likely fluid-responsive — a reasonable cue to give fluid (integrated with the clinical picture).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What does a large (>2–2.5 cm), plethoric, non-collapsing (<50%) IVC suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back:
High right atrial pressure / venous congestion —
  • fluid overload
  • right heart failure
  • cardiac tamponade
  • massive PE
  • tension pneumothorax
  • or pulmonary hypertension.
Do not flood with fluid.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Why does IVC respiratory variation reverse between spontaneous and mechanical ventilation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: In spontaneous breathing, inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure so the IVC collapses (collapsibility). In positive-pressure ventilation, inspiration raises intrathoracic pressure and distends the IVC (distensibility).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: List key limitations of IVC ultrasound for volume assessment.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back:
Unreliable with
  • high-pressure mechanical ventilation
  • raised intra-abdominal pressure
  • isolated RV failure
  • and in athletes.
It is a trend/adjunct used within RUSH/FoCUS alongside cardiac and lung POCUS — never a single number to treat in isolation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What formula estimates bladder volume on point-of-care ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: The ellipsoid estimate: volume (mL) ≈ height × width × depth × 0.52, using three orthogonal diameters in centimetres. Automated scanners compute this for you.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: How does a bladder scan distinguish urinary retention from anuria in an oliguric patient?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: A full, tense bladder (often >600 mL) = retention → catheterise. An empty bladder means it is NOT retention → look for a pre-renal/renal cause of anuria and avoid an unnecessary catheter.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What post-void residual (PVR) values are normal vs abnormal?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Normal PVR <50 mL; up to ~100 mL is often acceptable in the elderly. Persistently raised PVR indicates incomplete emptying — e.g. BPH/outlet obstruction, neurogenic bladder, or drugs (anticholinergics, opioids).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What causes a bladder scanner to over-read the volume?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: A large ovarian cyst, ascites, or a gravid uterus in the scanning field can be mistaken for bladder. If the volume is implausible, confirm with real-time ultrasound imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: On ultrasound, what does a full bladder look like?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: An anechoic (black) fluid-filled sac with posterior acoustic enhancement (a bright band behind it), because sound passes freely through the urine.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What does NICE recommend as the first-line method for central venous catheter insertion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: 2D ultrasound guidance — it is the preferred method, especially for internal jugular vein cannulation, giving higher first-pass success and fewer complications than the landmark technique.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: How do you distinguish a vein from an artery on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: The vein is compressible (collapses with gentle probe pressure), thin-walled, non-pulsatile, often larger, and augments with distal compression. The artery is round, thick-walled, pulsatile and non-compressible. Use colour/pulsed Doppler if unsure.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Contrast short-axis vs long-axis needle guidance.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Short-axis (out-of-plane): vessel is a circle, needle tip a bright dot — must track the tip down. Long-axis (in-plane): vessel is a tube, the whole needle shaft is visible in one plane for better depth control.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What must you confirm before dilating during central line insertion, and what checks follow?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Confirm the guidewire is in the VEIN (not the artery) before dilating. Afterwards check line tip position and exclude pneumothorax with CXR or lung ultrasound.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: How is inadvertent large-bore arterial cannulation managed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Do NOT remove the catheter and compress. Leave it in situ and get urgent vascular/surgical advice — pulling a large-bore arterial line risks catastrophic bleeding. Prevent it by confirming venous placement before dilating.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What is the Seldinger technique sequence for catheter-based drainage?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back:
Needle → guidewire → dilator → pigtail catheter.
  • Puncture the collection with a needle
  • thread a guidewire through
  • remove the needle
  • dilate the track over the wire
  • then railroad the pigtail catheter over the wire and remove the wire.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Which professional body recommends US guidance for pleural procedures, and why?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: The British Thoracic Society (BTS). US guidance markedly reduces the risk of organ puncture (liver, spleen, lung) and complications such as bleeding and pneumothorax compared with blind/landmark technique.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: Classic site for an ascitic tap/drain, and what must be avoided?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Left iliac fossa. Avoid the inferior epigastric vessels. Diagnostic paracentesis is used to investigate SBP; therapeutic drainage is used for large-volume/tense ascites.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: How does US help make a drainage/aspiration safer?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: It confirms the collection is present and its size, identifies a safe window, marks the depth to target, and keeps the needle away from bowel, vessels and solid organs — either real-time or via a marked site.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What is the management principle for an infected collection under pressure (e.g. pyonephrosis, empyema, septic abscess)?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Urgent drainage for source control ALONGSIDE antibiotics. Antibiotics alone are insufficient for an undrained infected/obstructed pocket; tense collections causing organ compromise (e.g. tamponade) need emergency drainage.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What do bilateral B-lines on lung ultrasound mean, and what should you do?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: ≥3 vertical comet-tail B-lines per field that are bilateral and diffuse indicate an interstitial syndrome — usually cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (also ARDS). Action: treat the oedema (sit up, oxygen, IV nitrate, IV furosemide) and do NOT give fluid. Focal B-lines suggest pneumonia/contusion instead.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.front: What must accompany a large-volume ascitic drain (paracentesis)?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.back: Human albumin solution (HAS) replacement — roughly 8 g albumin per litre drained beyond ~5 L — to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction. Mark/scan the site (usually left iliac fossa), avoiding the inferior epigastric vessels, organs and bowel.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Through which structure is neonatal cranial ultrasound performed, and what limits the window of opportunity?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Through the anterior fontanelle, which acts as an acoustic window. It only works while the fontanelle is open (closes ~9–18 months), so it is a neonatal/early-infancy tool.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Which infants are routinely screened with cranial ultrasound, and for what?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Preterm infants, especially <32 weeks or <1500 g, screened for germinal matrix/intraventricular haemorrhage (GMH-IVH) and white matter injury (PVL); also to assess ventricular size and hydrocephalus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: State the four grades of GMH-IVH on cranial ultrasound.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back:
• I: germinal matrix haemorrhage only.
  • II: IVH without ventricular dilatation.
  • III: IVH with ventricular dilatation.
  • IV: intraparenchymal haemorrhagic venous infarction.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What is periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) and its main clinical association?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: White matter injury of prematurity — periventricular echogenic 'flare' progressing to cystic change. Strongly associated with cerebral palsy (spastic diplegia).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Give two key limitations of cranial ultrasound and the preferred alternative.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Poor for the posterior fossa and for cortical/peripheral or subtle lesions. MRI is superior for anatomical detail, HIE prognostication and posterior fossa imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Why is ultrasound, rather than X-ray, the imaging of choice for DDH in infants under 4-6 months?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: The femoral head is still largely cartilaginous and has no ossific nucleus, so it is invisible on plain radiograph. Ultrasound images the cartilage directly and allows dynamic stability testing. Once the ossific nucleus appears (~4-6 months) radiographs take over.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Describe the Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back:
• Barlow: adduct and push posteriorly to detect a dislocatable hip.
  • Ortolani: abduct and lift to relocate a dislocated hip (a palpable clunk).
These are performed at the newborn and 6-8 week NIPE examination.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Which infants in the UK pathway receive an ultrasound hip?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back:
Babies with a positive NIPE examination (positive Barlow/Ortolani) OR risk factors:
  • breech presentation (especially at/after 36 weeks or at delivery)
  • first-degree family history of DDH
  • and in some pathways female sex, oligohydramnios, and firstborn status.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What does the Graf alpha angle measure and what is normal?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: The alpha angle measures the bony acetabular roof. Normal is ≥60 degrees; a lower angle indicates a shallow, dysplastic acetabulum. The beta angle measures the cartilaginous roof. Hips are graded type I (normal) to type IV (severe dysplasia/dislocation).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: First-line management of confirmed DDH in a young infant, and consequences if untreated?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: A Pavlik harness holds the hips flexed and abducted so the acetabulum develops around a reduced head. Failed or late cases need closed/open reduction and a spica cast. Untreated DDH leads to limp, leg-length discrepancy, and early osteoarthritis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Which imaging investigation confirms infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, and why is it preferred?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Ultrasound — it is the non-invasive investigation of choice, confirming the diagnosis in real time without radiation or contrast by directly imaging and measuring the hypertrophied pylorus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What are the two diagnostic ultrasound threshold measurements in IHPS?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back:
• Pyloric muscle wall thickness ≥3 mm (mnemonic "π / 3.14" ≈ 3 mm)
  • and pyloric channel length ≥15–17 mm.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What is the classic biochemical derangement in pyloric stenosis and its cause?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, caused by loss of gastric hydrochloric acid (H+ and Cl−) through persistent vomiting, with renal K+ wasting.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Name the classic sonographic signs of IHPS.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back:
• Transverse "target/doughnut" sign (hypoechoic thickened muscle around echogenic mucosa)
  • longitudinal elongated "cervix" sign
  • failure of gastric contents to pass through the channel
  • and a hyperperistaltic stomach.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Outline the correct management sequence for IHPS.
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Resuscitate first: correct fluid, electrolyte and acid-base derangement with IV fluids, replacing K+ and Cl− until the alkalosis resolves. Definitive treatment is Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, performed only once the baby is fully resuscitated.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What is the most common anatomical type of intussusception, and in what age group does it peak?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Ileocolic is the most common type. It typically affects infants/toddlers (~3 months–2 years) with a peak incidence around 6–9 months.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What are the classic ultrasound signs of intussusception?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: The TARGET / DOUGHNUT sign (concentric rings of bowel-within-bowel) on transverse imaging, and the PSEUDOKIDNEY sign on longitudinal imaging. US is the first-line diagnostic test.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What is the first-line therapeutic management of stable intussusception with no perforation or peritonitis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Resuscitate (IV fluids, NG tube), then AIR (pneumatic) ENEMA reduction under radiological guidance — it is both diagnostic and therapeutic. A contrast enema is the alternative.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What is 'redcurrant jelly' stool and what does it signify?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Stool containing blood and mucus. It is a LATE and ominous sign of bowel ischaemia — its absence does not exclude intussusception, and clinicians should not wait for it before imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: What are the contraindications to enema reduction that mandate urgent surgery?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back:
• Peritonitis
  • perforation (free air)
  • and shock.
Surgery is also required if the enema fails or a pathological lead point is present.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: How are neonatal intraventricular haemorrhage and its main complication managed?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: There is no acute cure for the bleed — management is supportive with serial cranial ultrasound to detect post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus. Rising ventricular size/head circumference is managed by serial LPs or a ventricular access device, progressing to a VP shunt if it persists. Periventricular leukomalacia needs developmental follow-up.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.front: Why is hip ultrasound for DDH done at around 6 weeks rather than at birth?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Paediatric.back: Before ~6 weeks many hips are physiologically immature, so early scanning over-calls dysplasia and leads to unnecessary treatment. US is used under ~4–6 months (before the femoral head ossifies); after that an X-ray is used. Selective scanning is offered for breech presentation and a family history (UK NIPE).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A gallbladder ultrasound shows a bright (hyperechoic) focus with a dark band extending deep to it that moves with position. What is this appearance?
options: Anechoic cyst with posterior acoustic enhancement
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A bright, mobile focus casting an acoustic shadow (dark band behind it) is the classic appearance of a gallstone. Shadowing occurs because the stone strongly reflects/absorbs sound so little passes deep to it.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: Which of the following is a recognised LIMITATION of abdominal ultrasound?
options: It cannot be performed at the bedside
It provides an excellent view of the retroperitoneal pancreas
It is highly operator-dependent and limited by bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: It is highly operator-dependent and limited by bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: US is operator-dependent and easily obscured by bowel gas and obesity, and is poor for the retroperitoneum/pancreas. It uses NO ionising radiation, is safe in pregnancy, and can be done at the bedside — those are advantages, not limitations.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A structure appears completely black (anechoic) with increased brightness in the tissues immediately behind it. This is most consistent with:
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Anechoic (black) content with posterior acoustic enhancement (brightening deep to it) indicates a simple fluid-filled structure such as a cyst. Calcification and gas cause shadowing, not enhancement; fibrosis and fat are echogenic, not anechoic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 55-year-old with type 2 diabetes has mildly deranged LFTs. Ultrasound shows a liver that is diffusely brighter than the right kidney, with poor visualisation of the deep hepatic vessels and diaphragm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A diffusely bright/hyperechoic liver with posterior beam attenuation and loss of vessel and diaphragm clarity is the classic "bright liver" of steatosis/NAFLD, strongly associated with type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A patient with known alcohol-related cirrhosis attends for routine 6-monthly surveillance ultrasound. A new 2 cm solid nodule is identified that was not present previously. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the liver
Reassure and repeat ultrasound in 5 years
No action as this is a simple cyst
Commence oral antibiotics for a liver abscess
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Arrange contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the liver
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A new focal solid lesion in a cirrhotic liver is hepatocellular carcinoma until proven otherwise. Ultrasound detects it but cannot characterise it, so multiphase contrast-enhanced CT or MRI is required.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: Which ultrasound appearance is most characteristic of a simple hepatic cyst?
options: Anechoic lesion with a thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement
Coarse nodular parenchyma with a shrunken outline
Bright liver with posterior beam attenuation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Anechoic lesion with a thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A simple cyst is anechoic (fluid-filled, black) with an imperceptibly thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement. The uniformly hyperechoic lesion describes a haemangioma, and the "target" lesion describes a metastasis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 45-year-old woman with colicky RUQ pain has an ultrasound showing a bright, echogenic focus in the gallbladder lumen that casts a dark band beneath it and rolls to the dependent side when she is repositioned. What is the single most specific feature confirming this is a gallstone?
options: Posterior acoustic shadowing with mobility on repositioning
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Posterior acoustic shadowing with mobility on repositioning
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Brightness alone can be seen with polyps or sludge. The combination of posterior acoustic shadowing (the stone reflects/absorbs the beam) plus mobility with gravity is what reliably identifies a gallstone and distinguishes it from a fixed polyp or non-shadowing sludge.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 60-year-old man has RUQ pain and fever. Ultrasound shows a distended gallbladder with a 5 mm thick wall, a rim of pericholecystic fluid, a stone lodged in the gallbladder neck, and maximal tenderness as the probe presses over the gallbladder. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Wall thickening >3 mm, pericholecystic fluid, distension, a stone impacted in the neck and a positive sonographic Murphy's sign are the hallmark features of acute cholecystitis. Biliary colic has no inflammatory signs; cholangitis is characterised by jaundice with duct dilatation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A patient presents with fever, RUQ pain and jaundice. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct at 9 mm but no visible duct stone. What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?
options: Reassure and repeat ultrasound in 6 weeks
Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the next available list
Oral ursodeoxycholic acid to dissolve stones
IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: IV antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Fever, RUQ pain and jaundice is Charcot's triad — ascending cholangitis, an infected obstructed biliary tree and a medical emergency. It requires prompt IV antibiotics and urgent decompression of the biliary system, typically by ERCP. A non-visualised duct stone does not exclude obstruction, as ultrasound is insensitive for CBD stones.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 52-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain and a serum lipase three times the upper limit of normal. He is admitted with acute pancreatitis. What is the chief reason an abdominal ultrasound is requested?
options: To confirm the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis
To assess the pancreas for necrosis
To measure the severity score of pancreatitis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Diagnosis of acute pancreatitis is clinical plus raised amylase/lipase, not imaging. US is used chiefly to look for gallstones and a dilated CBD (gallstone pancreatitis). CT — not US — assesses necrosis and severity, ideally at 48–72h.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 60-year-old woman has painless obstructive jaundice and 6 kg of weight loss. Ultrasound shows dilatation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct. Which is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat ultrasound in 6 months
Urgent CT and/or endoscopic ultrasound referral
ERCP alone with no cross-sectional imaging
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Urgent CT and/or endoscopic ultrasound referral
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: The double-duct sign with painless obstructive jaundice and weight loss strongly suggests pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. US may raise the suspicion, but CT and EUS are far superior for detection, staging and biopsy, so urgent referral is needed.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: An ultrasound of a patient with a long history of alcohol excess shows an atrophic pancreas with echogenic foci that cast acoustic shadows and a dilated pancreatic duct. Which diagnosis do these features best fit?
options: Normal pancreas obscured by bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Atrophy, calcifications (echogenic foci with shadowing) and a dilated pancreatic duct are the classic US features of chronic pancreatitis. An anechoic collection would suggest a pseudocyst, and a focal hypoechoic mass would suggest adenocarcinoma.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 19-year-old with sore throat, fever and fatigue has a positive monospot test. Ultrasound shows a homogeneously enlarged, soft spleen measuring 15 cm. Which advice is most important?
options: Avoid contact sports until recovery due to rupture risk
Repeat ultrasound daily until the spleen normalises
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Avoid contact sports until recovery due to rupture risk
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) causes an enlarged, fragile spleen prone to rupture. The key safety advice is to avoid contact sports (typically ~3–4 weeks/until recovery). Splenectomy and anticoagulation are not indicated, and antibiotics do not treat this viral illness.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: A 25-year-old is brought in after a road traffic collision with LUQ pain and a heart rate of 130 with systolic BP 80 mmHg. FAST shows free fluid in the splenorenal recess. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: CT abdomen with contrast to grade the injury
Immediate resuscitation and transfer to theatre
MRI abdomen to characterise the spleen
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.answer: Immediate resuscitation and transfer to theatre
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A positive FAST in a haemodynamically UNSTABLE trauma patient is a surgical emergency. Resuscitate and go to theatre without delay — CT is only appropriate for the haemodynamically stable patient to grade injury and plan conservative management.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.question: During an abdominal ultrasound, a 2 cm rounded nodule with the same echotexture as the spleen is seen adjacent to the splenic hilum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Abdomen.explanation: A splenunculus is a common normal variant: a small round nodule near the hilum with echotexture identical to the spleen. It should not be mistaken for a mass or lymph node. An infarct is wedge-shaped and hypoechoic, a cyst is anechoic, and an abscess is a complex collection in a septic patient.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 72-year-old man presents with anuria and a creatinine that has tripled over 48 hours. Renal ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis, a grossly distended bladder and a post-void residual of 900 mL. What is the most likely mechanism of his AKI?
options: Bladder outlet obstruction causing post-renal AKI
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Bladder outlet obstruction causing post-renal AKI
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: Bilateral hydronephrosis with a chronically distended bladder and a large post-void residual localises the obstruction to the bladder outlet (e.g. prostatic enlargement). This is post-renal AKI; catheterisation relieves the obstruction. Pre-renal and intrinsic causes do not produce hydronephrosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A renal ultrasound performed for flank pain demonstrates a bright echogenic focus in the renal pelvis with clean posterior acoustic shadowing, and mild ipsilateral hydronephrosis. Ureteric colic is suspected but no ureteric stone is seen. What is the best next investigation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: The echogenic focus with posterior shadowing is a stone. US is insensitive for ureteric stones, so a non-contrast CT KUB is the most sensitive test to confirm a ureteric calculus, locate it and guide management. It also detects the stone burden US cannot visualise along the ureter.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: During an ultrasound for haematuria, a 3 cm heterogeneous solid mass is found arising from the upper pole of the right kidney. It shows no posterior acoustic enhancement. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure — this is a simple cyst
Arrange contrast-enhanced CT for characterisation and staging, and refer to urology
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Arrange contrast-enhanced CT for characterisation and staging, and refer to urology
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: A solid renal mass is a possible renal cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. The absence of posterior enhancement argues against a simple cyst. Contrast CT characterises and stages the lesion and urology referral is required. Angiomyolipoma (echogenic fat) is a differential but still needs CT to confirm macroscopic fat.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 66-year-old man attends AAA screening. His abdominal ultrasound shows an infrarenal aortic diameter of 4.8 cm. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Immediate referral for elective open repair
Urgent CT angiography to exclude rupture
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: A medium AAA (4.5–5.4 cm) is placed on 3-monthly ultrasound surveillance. It has not reached the 5.5 cm threshold for elective repair, and the patient is asymptomatic and stable, so CT is not indicated.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 74-year-old man collapses with sudden severe back pain. He is hypotensive with a pulsatile abdominal mass and a known 6 cm AAA. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Immediate transfer to theatre for emergency repair
CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis before any intervention
Repeat outpatient ultrasound to confirm expansion
Commence antihypertensives and reassess in 24 hours
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Immediate transfer to theatre for emergency repair
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: The triad of sudden pain, pulsatile mass and hypotension indicates a ruptured AAA. A haemodynamically unstable patient must go straight to theatre — imaging must not delay definitive surgery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: Which statement about the role of ultrasound in AAA is most accurate?
options: Ultrasound is the definitive test for pre-operative EVAR planning
Ultrasound is used to diagnose rupture in unstable patients before theatre
Ultrasound is radiation-free, cheap and reliably measures maximal aortic diameter
An AAA is defined as an aortic diameter ≥2 cm on ultrasound
Ultrasound cannot detect mural thrombus within the aneurysm sac
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Ultrasound is radiation-free, cheap and reliably measures maximal aortic diameter
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: These properties make US ideal for screening and surveillance. CT angiography — not US — is used for pre-operative planning and to diagnose rupture in stable patients. An AAA is ≥3 cm, and US does show mural thrombus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 58-year-old man with known alcoholic cirrhosis presents with a distended abdomen. Bedside ultrasound is requested to confirm ascites. In a supine patient, which single site is the most sensitive for detecting a small volume of free fluid?
options: The subphrenic space above the spleen
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: In a supine patient, Morison's pouch — the potential space between the liver and right kidney — is the most dependent upper-abdominal recess and the most sensitive location for detecting small volumes of free fluid, which appears as an anechoic stripe. This is also a key window in the FAST scan.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A cirrhotic patient with new ascites undergoes a diagnostic tap. The ascitic fluid appears clear on ultrasound (uniformly anechoic). Serum albumin is 30 g/L and ascitic albumin is 15 g/L. What does this indicate?
options: Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 15 g/L, indicating a malignant exudate
Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 15 g/L, indicating portal hypertension
Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 45 g/L, indicating infection
A low gradient consistent with peritoneal TB
An indeterminate gradient requiring cytology to classify
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Serum-ascites albumin gradient of 15 g/L, indicating portal hypertension
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: SAAG = 30 − 15 = 15 g/L. A SAAG ≥11 g/L reliably indicates portal hypertension (here from cirrhosis), producing a transudate that is typically uniformly anechoic on ultrasound. A low gradient (<11 g/L) would instead point to exudative causes such as malignancy or infection.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 62-year-old woman with cirrhosis presents with fever, diffuse abdominal pain and new confusion. Ultrasound confirms a moderate volume of ascites. A diagnostic tap is performed. Which finding confirms the most important diagnosis to exclude?
options: Positive ascitic fluid cytology for malignant cells
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: Fever, abdominal pain and encephalopathy in a cirrhotic strongly suggest spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), a medical emergency. SBP is diagnosed by an ascitic polymorphonuclear (neutrophil) count ≥250/mm³ and requires prompt empirical antibiotics. The other findings relate to classifying the ascites but do not diagnose SBP.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 9-year-old boy has 24 hours of central pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, anorexia and a low-grade fever. Diagnosis is uncertain and imaging is requested. Which first-line investigation is most appropriate?
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: In children, US is first-line imaging as it avoids ionising radiation. CT would be reserved for equivocal cases where suspicion persists after US.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: Which ultrasound finding is most specific for acute appendicitis?
options: A compressible tubular structure measuring 4 mm
Free fluid in the pouch of Douglas alone
A blind-ending, non-compressible tube from the caecal pole measuring >6 mm
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: A blind-ending, non-compressible tube from the caecal pole measuring >6 mm
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: The diagnostic combination is a blind-ending, non-compressible, aperistaltic tube >6 mm. A compressible 4 mm structure is normal, and a non-visualised appendix does not confirm or exclude the diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.question: A 26-year-old woman with RIF pain has an ultrasound that fails to visualise the appendix, but her pain and localised peritonism persist. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the same ultrasound in one week
Immediately start long-term oral antibiotics at home
Escalate to CT or proceed to observation / diagnostic laparoscopy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.answer: Escalate to CT or proceed to observation / diagnostic laparoscopy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Renal, Aorta.explanation: A non-visualised appendix does not exclude appendicitis. With persisting suspicion, further imaging (CT in a non-pregnant adult) or observation/diagnostic laparoscopy is indicated; discharge would be unsafe.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 24-year-old woman attends for a routine transabdominal pelvic ultrasound. The sonographer asks her to drink water and hold her urine beforehand. What is the primary reason a full bladder is required?
options: It compresses the ovaries to make them easier to measure
It reduces patient movement during the scan
It provides an acoustic window and displaces bowel gas from the pelvis
It increases blood flow to the uterus for Doppler assessment
It is needed to calculate an accurate post-void residual volume
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: It provides an acoustic window and displaces bowel gas from the pelvis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A distended, fluid-filled bladder transmits ultrasound (acoustic window) and pushes gas-filled bowel out of the pelvis, allowing the pelvic organs to be visualised. Without it the scan is often non-diagnostic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: Which of the following is a recognised limitation of transabdominal pelvic ultrasound compared with the transvaginal approach?
options: It cannot be used in children
It is invasive and poorly tolerated
It cannot visualise large masses that extend out of the pelvis
It requires an empty bladder to work well
It has lower resolution and is degraded by obesity and bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: It has lower resolution and is degraded by obesity and bowel gas
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: TAUS is non-invasive and well tolerated and is actually better for large extra-pelvic masses, but its resolution is lower than transvaginal scanning and image quality is reduced by obesity, bowel gas and an empty bladder.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 27-year-old woman presents with acute right iliac fossa pain and a positive pregnancy test. A transabdominal ultrasound performed with a partially filled bladder appears unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure the patient that the scan excludes an ectopic pregnancy
Proceed to transvaginal ultrasound for higher-resolution assessment
Discharge with a routine outpatient follow-up scan in 6 weeks
Repeat the transabdominal scan in 24 hours only
Arrange a CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Proceed to transvaginal ultrasound for higher-resolution assessment
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A technically limited or normal-appearing TAUS does not exclude an ectopic pregnancy. The correct step is to proceed to transvaginal ultrasound, which gives a higher-resolution close-up view of the adnexa and uterus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 32-year-old woman with 6 weeks amenorrhoea and a positive pregnancy test is booked for transvaginal ultrasound. What bladder preparation should she be given?
options: Drink 1 litre of water and attend with a full bladder
Bladder state is irrelevant for transvaginal scanning
Empty her bladder before the scan
Take a diuretic one hour before
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Empty her bladder before the scan
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: TVUS is performed with an empty bladder, the opposite of transabdominal scanning. A full bladder displaces the pelvic organs out of the high-frequency probe's near field and degrades the close-up image.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 58-year-old woman presents with postmenopausal bleeding. TVUS shows an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. What is the most appropriate next step?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. A stripe of 4 mm or less is reassuring, but a thickened endometrium (here 9 mm) requires hysteroscopy and biopsy for histological diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 29-year-old woman has a positive pregnancy test and serum hCG of 2200 IU/L. TVUS shows an empty uterus with a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. What does this most likely represent?
options: A normal very early intrauterine pregnancy
A completed miscarriage requiring no follow-up
Ectopic pregnancy / pregnancy of unknown location until proven otherwise
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Ectopic pregnancy / pregnancy of unknown location until proven otherwise
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: With hCG above the discriminatory zone (~1500 IU/L) an intrauterine sac should be visible. An empty uterus with positive hCG is a pregnancy of unknown location and must be treated as ectopic until proven otherwise — gynae review and serial hCG. Free fluid heightens the concern.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 63-year-old woman presents with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 9 mm. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as the bleeding is due to atrophy
Start topical vaginal oestrogen and review
Arrange a transabdominal ultrasound for confirmation
Refer on a 2-week-wait pathway for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Refer on a 2-week-wait pathway for hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Postmenopausal bleeding with an endometrium >4 mm is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Tissue diagnosis is mandatory via urgent (2-week-wait) hysteroscopy and endometrial biopsy; ultrasound alone cannot exclude carcinoma.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: Which transvaginal ultrasound appearance is most characteristic of adenomyosis rather than a fibroid?
options: A well-defined rounded hypoechoic mass with acoustic shadowing
A diffusely enlarged globular uterus with heterogeneous myometrium and a poorly defined junctional zone
A focal echogenic intracavity lesion with a feeding vessel
A bright shadowing linear echo in the central cavity
A single external fundal contour with an internal septum
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: A diffusely enlarged globular uterus with heterogeneous myometrium and a poorly defined junctional zone
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Adenomyosis is diffuse: a globular uterus, heterogeneous myometrium (often with myometrial cysts) and an ill-defined/thickened junctional zone, with no discrete mass. The well-defined shadowing mass describes a fibroid; the intracavity lesion with a feeding vessel is a polyp; the bright shadowing linear echo is an IUCD; the internal septum describes a septate uterus.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: During which part of the menstrual cycle is the premenopausal endometrium typically thinnest on ultrasound?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: The endometrium is thinnest and brightest just after menses in the early proliferative phase, then progressively thickens to become maximal and most echogenic in the secretory (luteal) phase. This cyclical variation means there is no single normal thickness premenopausally.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 24-year-old woman has a 4 cm right adnexal cyst on transvaginal ultrasound: anechoic, thin-walled, no septations, with posterior acoustic enhancement. She is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure; this is a simple functional cyst — repeat ultrasound in 6–12 weeks
Commence the combined oral contraceptive pill to shrink the cyst
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Reassure; this is a simple functional cyst — repeat ultrasound in 6–12 weeks
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Anechoic, thin-walled cysts with posterior enhancement and no solid or septated components are simple functional cysts. In a young asymptomatic woman these are almost always benign and resolve; interval rescan confirms resolution. CA-125/RMI and oncology referral are for complex/suspicious masses.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 15-year-old presents with sudden severe left iliac fossa pain and vomiting. Ultrasound shows an enlarged oedematous left ovary with peripherally displaced follicles; colour Doppler demonstrates preserved arterial flow. What is the correct next step?
options: Reassure — preserved Doppler flow excludes torsion
Discharge with analgesia and outpatient follow-up
Start IV antibiotics for pelvic inflammatory disease
Request an outpatient MRI to characterise the mass
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: The clinical picture and enlarged oedematous ovary with peripheralised follicles indicate torsion. Because of dual blood supply, Doppler flow may persist — a normal Doppler does not exclude torsion. Torsion is an emergency; urgent laparoscopy to detorse can save the ovary.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 58-year-old post-menopausal woman has a complex right ovarian mass with solid areas, thick septations and moderate ascites. CA-125 is 480 U/mL. Which statement about her assessment is correct?
options: Polycystic ovarian morphology explains these findings
Her RMI is low because she is post-menopausal
The ground-glass echoes confirm a benign endometrioma
The mass should simply be rescanned in 6 weeks
She has a high RMI and needs gynae-oncology MDT referral
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: She has a high RMI and needs gynae-oncology MDT referral
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: RMI = U × M × CA-125. Post-menopausal status scores M = 3 (increasing, not lowering, the index), the ultrasound features (solid areas, multilocular, ascites) give a high U score, and CA-125 is markedly raised — yielding an RMI well above 200. This mandates referral to the gynae-oncology MDT.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 27-year-old woman is 6 weeks by dates with light bleeding. TVUS shows an empty uterus. Her serum hCG is 2100 IU/L. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Normal early intrauterine pregnancy, reassure and discharge
hCG above the discriminatory zone with an empty uterus — ectopic must be actively excluded
Complete miscarriage, no further action needed
Threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: hCG above the discriminatory zone with an empty uterus — ectopic must be actively excluded
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: With serum hCG above ~1500 IU/L an intrauterine sac should be visible transvaginally. An empty uterus at this level is a pregnancy of unknown location that raises strong suspicion of ectopic; examine the adnexa and pouch of Douglas and consider serial hCG. It cannot be assumed normal, complete, or viable, and there are no molar features described.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: TVUS in a woman with a positive pregnancy test shows an intrauterine gestational sac with a mean sac diameter of 27 mm and no fetal pole. What does this indicate?
options: Viable intrauterine pregnancy, rescan not required
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A mean gestational sac diameter ≥25 mm with no fetal pole (an empty sac) meets the criterion for a non-viable pregnancy. Because the sac is intrauterine and eccentric this is a miscarriage, not an ectopic pseudosac. A CRL ≥7 mm with no heartbeat is the other non-viable criterion; below these thresholds one would rescan in 7–14 days.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A 31-year-old woman collapses at home. She has a positive pregnancy test, is tachycardic and hypotensive, reports right shoulder-tip pain, and has abdominal tenderness. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Resuscitate and arrange urgent gynaecology review and theatre without delaying for imaging
Arrange an outpatient TVUS before any intervention
Repeat serum hCG in 48 hours and review
Reassure and arrange EPAU follow-up in one week
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Resuscitate and arrange urgent gynaecology review and theatre without delaying for imaging
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: This is a haemodynamically unstable ruptured ectopic — a life-threatening surgical emergency. Positive pregnancy test, shock, and shoulder-tip pain (diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum) demand immediate resuscitation with large-bore IV access, cross-match, and urgent gynaecology/theatre. Imaging, serial hCG, methotrexate, or outpatient follow-up would dangerously delay definitive surgical control of bleeding.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A bladder scanner measures a bladder as 8 cm (height) × 6 cm × 5 cm on three orthogonal diameters. Using the ellipsoid formula, which value best approximates the volume?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: Bladder volume ≈ length × width × depth × 0.52 = 8 × 6 × 5 × 0.52 ≈ 125 mL. The ~240 mL distractor is the raw product (8×6×5) without the 0.52 ellipsoid correction factor.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: An 80-year-old man voids and is scanned immediately, showing a post-void residual of 40 mL. How should this be interpreted?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: A PVR <50 mL indicates normal emptying. Up to ~100 mL may be acceptable in the elderly; 40 mL is reassuring and needs no intervention.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.question: A frail woman presents with painless abdominal distension, oliguria and a creatinine that has doubled. Bladder scan shows a grossly distended thick-walled bladder and renal views show bilateral hydronephrosis. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Urgent urethral catheterisation with monitoring for post-obstructive diuresis
Start a fluid restriction and diuretics
Give a bolus of intravenous antibiotics
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.answer: Urgent urethral catheterisation with monitoring for post-obstructive diuresis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Pelvic & Gyn.explanation: This is high-pressure chronic retention causing obstructive AKI. Urgent catheterisation relieves the obstruction; afterwards watch for post-obstructive diuresis and electrolyte shifts, which can be marked.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A woman attends her first routine antenatal ultrasound at 12 weeks. Which measurement will be used to date the pregnancy most accurately?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: In the first trimester the crown-rump length (reliable ~8.5–14 weeks) is the single most accurate dating measurement. Head circumference and femur length are used later once CRL becomes unreliable beyond ~14 weeks.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: On a dating scan a twin pregnancy shows a triangular wedge of placental tissue extending between the two membranes at their insertion. What does this indicate?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: The triangular placental wedge is the lambda (twin-peak) sign, indicating dichorionicity (separate placentas). A flat T-sign, where the membrane meets the placenta at a right angle with no wedge, indicates monochorionicity.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: At a 12-week dating scan a single fetus with a fetal pole of appropriate size is seen, but no cardiac activity can be identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: A fetal pole of expected size with no detectable heartbeat suggests a missed miscarriage. This typically warrants a repeat scan and specialist review before management decisions.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: Which of the following is NOT a primary purpose of the UK dating scan?
options: Accurately dating the pregnancy and setting the EDD
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: The dating scan confirms viability and location, dates the pregnancy by CRL, establishes chorionicity in twins, and screens for gross anomalies. Fetal sex is not a purpose of the dating scan and is not reliably determined this early.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: Why must chorionicity be established at the first-trimester dating scan rather than later in pregnancy?
options: Chorionicity is assessed most accurately in the first trimester and determines the risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
Fetal heartbeat can only be seen in the first trimester
Nuchal translucency cannot be measured after the first trimester
CRL is only measurable after 14 weeks
The placenta has not yet formed later in pregnancy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.answer: Chorionicity is assessed most accurately in the first trimester and determines the risk of twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: The lambda and T-signs are clearest in the first trimester, and identifying monochorionicity is critical because those twins share a placenta and risk twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, requiring increased surveillance.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A woman attends for her first-trimester combined screening test. Which combination of markers is characteristically associated with trisomy 21?
options: Increased NT, low β-hCG, high PAPP-A
Decreased NT, high β-hCG, high PAPP-A
Increased NT, high β-hCG, low PAPP-A
Increased NT, low β-hCG, low PAPP-A
Decreased NT, low β-hCG, high PAPP-A
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.answer: Increased NT, high β-hCG, low PAPP-A
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: In trisomy 21 the combined test typically shows an increased nuchal translucency, raised β-hCG and reduced PAPP-A. These are integrated with maternal age to give a risk figure.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A woman is 16+3 weeks pregnant at her booking appointment, having missed the NT window. What screening is now appropriate?
options: Chorionic villus sampling as first-line screen
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: NT can only be measured 11+2 to 14+1 weeks. After the window, the quadruple test (14–20 weeks) is offered — it screens for trisomy 21 only. CVS is a diagnostic, not screening, test.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A combined test returns a chance of 1 in 90 for trisomy 21. Which statement is most accurate when counselling the woman?
options: The fetus definitely has Down syndrome
This is a higher-chance result and she is offered further testing including NIPT or diagnostic CVS/amniocentesis
She should proceed straight to amniocentesis with no other options
The screening test itself carries a 1% miscarriage risk
A normal NT excludes any need for further discussion
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.answer: This is a higher-chance result and she is offered further testing including NIPT or diagnostic CVS/amniocentesis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: A result more likely than the 1 in 150 cut-off is higher-chance and prompts the offer of NIPT (non-invasive) or diagnostic CVS/amniocentesis. Screening estimates chance and carries no procedure risk; only the invasive diagnostic tests carry the ~0.5–1% miscarriage risk.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A woman attends for her routine anomaly scan. Within which gestational window does the UK Fetal Anomaly Screening Programme offer this scan?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: FASP offers the mid-trimester anomaly scan between 18+0 and 20+6 weeks. The 11+2–14+1 window is for the combined test and dating/nuchal translucency, not the structural anomaly survey.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: At the 20-week scan the sonographer notes anhydramnios with an absent fetal bladder and non-visualised kidneys. Which diagnosis does this combination most strongly suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Absent kidneys and bladder with anhydramnios (the liquor is largely fetal urine) point to bilateral renal agenesis, a lethal anomaly producing the Potter sequence, requiring urgent fetal medicine referral.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A 20-week scan shows an isolated echogenic intracardiac focus with otherwise normal anatomy. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: It is a structural cardiac defect requiring surgery
It is a soft marker that may prompt review of aneuploidy risk
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.answer: It is a soft marker that may prompt review of aneuploidy risk
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: An echogenic intracardiac focus is a soft marker, not a structural defect. In isolation it is weakly associated with trisomy 21 and is interpreted alongside the woman's prior combined-test risk; it is neither diagnostic nor an indication for termination.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A 34-week fetus has an AC on the 5th centile with HC preserved on the 40th centile, and umbilical artery Doppler shows absent end-diastolic flow. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and rebook a routine growth scan in 4 weeks
Advise the mother to increase oral fluid intake and rescan liquor in a week
Commence oral iron and repeat SFH measurement at the next community appointment
Discharge to routine midwifery care as the head circumference is normal
Refer for fetal medicine input with steroids and consideration of timed delivery
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.answer: Refer for fetal medicine input with steroids and consideration of timed delivery
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Asymmetric growth restriction (low AC, spared HC) with absent end-diastolic flow indicates significant placental insufficiency and a real stillbirth risk. This warrants fetal medicine involvement, antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity, and planning for timed delivery — not a routine interval scan.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: Which biometry measurement is regarded as the most sensitive single indicator of fetal growth restriction?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: AC reflects fetal liver glycogen stores and subcutaneous fat, both of which are depleted early in placental insufficiency. It is the most sensitive individual measurement and typically falls before HC, producing the asymmetric head-sparing pattern.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A woman with poorly controlled gestational diabetes has a growth scan showing an EFW on the 95th centile with a large abdominal circumference. Which complication is she most at risk of at delivery?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Fetal hyperinsulinaemia in maternal diabetes drives macrosomia (EFW >90th centile) with a disproportionately large abdomen and shoulders. This substantially increases the risk of shoulder dystocia during vaginal delivery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A growth-restricted fetus at 29 weeks has umbilical artery Doppler showing flow that reverses below the baseline during diastole. What does this finding indicate?
options: Reversed end-diastolic flow indicating critical placental compromise
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.answer: Reversed end-diastolic flow indicating critical placental compromise
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Diastolic flow dipping below the baseline in the umbilical artery is reversed end-diastolic flow (REDF), the most advanced arterial sign of severe placental insufficiency. It carries a high risk of hypoxia and stillbirth and mandates urgent fetal medicine review, corticosteroids and consideration of delivery.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A fetus with red-cell alloimmunisation is being monitored. Which Doppler parameter is used to detect significant fetal anaemia and time intrauterine transfusion?
options: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.answer: Middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Fetal anaemia lowers blood viscosity and produces a hyperdynamic circulation, raising MCA peak systolic velocity (PSV). A value above 1.5 multiples of the median is the recognised trigger for intrauterine transfusion. The other parameters assess placental resistance, redistribution or cardiac decompensation, not anaemia.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A hypoxic growth-restricted fetus shows a falling middle cerebral artery pulsatility index. What does this represent?
options: Placental insufficiency of the maternal side
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: A hypoxic fetus preferentially redistributes cardiac output to the brain. Cerebral vasodilation reduces resistance and therefore lowers the MCA pulsatility index — the brain-sparing effect. This is an early adaptive marker of centralisation, best interpreted alongside the umbilical artery via the cerebroplacental ratio.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: A 34-week high-risk pregnancy undergoes a biophysical profile. Fetal breathing, gross movements, tone and CTG are all normal, but the deepest amniotic fluid pool is 1.4 cm. What is the total BPP score?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Four components are normal (2 each = 8) but the amniotic fluid component scores 0 because the deepest vertical pool is <2 cm (oligohydramnios). Total = 8. This is still reassuring numerically, but the oligohydramnios reflects chronic placental insufficiency and warrants closer surveillance.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: Which component of the biophysical profile primarily reflects CHRONIC placental function rather than acute fetal oxygenation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Amniotic fluid volume reflects chronic placental function: sustained hypoxia redistributes blood away from the fetal kidneys, reducing urine output and causing oligohydramnios. The other four are acute markers driven by CNS activity and change over minutes to hours.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.question: According to the concept of gradual hypoxia, which biophysical activity is typically preserved the LONGEST and is lost only in severe fetal compromise?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Obstetric.explanation: Fetal tone is controlled by the earliest-developing CNS centres, which are most resistant to hypoxia, so it is lost last. CTG reactivity and breathing movements are the most hypoxia-sensitive and are lost first. Amniotic fluid is a chronic marker, not part of this acute sequence.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 62-year-old presents with a swollen, painful right calf. On bedside ultrasound the common femoral vein does not collapse when the probe is pressed until the adjacent artery deforms. Which single feature is the cardinal diagnostic sign of DVT?
options: Distension of the vein relative to the artery
Failure of augmentation on calf squeeze
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Non-compressibility of the vein
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: A normal vein flattens completely under gentle probe pressure; a vein held open by thrombus will not compress. This is the cardinal, near-diagnostic sign. The other features are supportive but non-compressibility is decisive.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A patient scores 1 on the two-level Wells score ("DVT unlikely"). According to the UK/NICE pathway, what is the correct next step?
options: Proximal leg vein ultrasound within 4 hours
D-dimer, proceeding to ultrasound only if positive
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: D-dimer, proceeding to ultrasound only if positive
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: For "DVT unlikely" (Wells ≤1), NICE recommends a D-dimer first; a negative result excludes DVT, while a positive result leads on to proximal ultrasound. Immediate US within 4 hours is the pathway for "DVT likely" (≥2).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A patient with iliofemoral DVT develops a massively swollen, tense, blue and intensely painful leg. Which diagnosis and action is most appropriate?
options: Ruptured Baker's cyst — arrange outpatient MRI
Phlegmasia cerulea dolens — urgent vascular review and consider thrombolysis
Superficial thrombophlebitis — reassure and give NSAIDs
Chronic venous insufficiency — prescribe compression stockings
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Phlegmasia cerulea dolens — urgent vascular review and consider thrombolysis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Extensive iliofemoral thrombosis causing a swollen, blue, painful leg is phlegmasia cerulea dolens — venous outflow obstruction compromising arterial inflow.
