It is limb-threatening and needs urgent vascular surgery input with consideration of thrombolysis or thrombectomy.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 68-year-old man has a right-sided amaurosis fugax and dysphasia 3 days ago that fully resolved. Carotid Doppler shows a right ICA PSV of 260 cm/s, EDV 110 cm/s and an ICA/CCA ratio of 4.5, consistent with 70–99% NASCET stenosis. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure and repeat the scan in 6 months
Best medical therapy alone with no surgical referral
Refer for carotid endarterectomy only if he develops further symptoms
Refer for carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks
Anticoagulate with warfarin and avoid any intervention
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Refer for carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: This is symptomatic (recent TIA in the ipsilateral carotid territory) severe stenosis (70–99% NASCET). Symptomatic 50–99% stenosis is an indication for carotid endarterectomy, and it should be performed as soon as possible — ideally within 2 weeks of symptom onset — because early recurrent stroke risk is high. Best medical therapy is given in addition, not instead.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: On carotid Doppler, which finding indicates the TIGHTEST degree of internal carotid artery stenosis?
options: ICA peak systolic velocity of 260 cm/s with EDV 120 cm/s
ICA peak systolic velocity of 80 cm/s
Absent flow on B-mode with a low-velocity trickle (string sign)
Smooth wall with intima-media thickening but no plaque
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: ICA peak systolic velocity of 260 cm/s with EDV 120 cm/s
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Velocity rises as the lumen narrows, so the high PSV (260 cm/s) with elevated EDV represents a severe (~70–99%) stenosis. The string sign reflects a near-occlusion where velocities are paradoxically LOW because flow is critically reduced, so it is not the tightest patent stenosis by velocity criteria. 80 cm/s is normal and IMT without plaque is minimal disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 72-year-old woman is found on carotid Doppler to have an asymptomatic 65% stenosis of the left ICA during investigation for hypertension. She has never had a TIA or stroke. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Best medical therapy: antiplatelet, statin, BP control and smoking cessation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Best medical therapy: antiplatelet, statin, BP control and smoking cessation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Asymptomatic carotid stenosis is managed predominantly medically — antiplatelet therapy, a high-intensity statin, blood pressure control, and smoking cessation — because the stroke-prevention benefit of surgery in asymptomatic patients is modest and does not warrant urgent intervention. The 2-week surgical pathway applies to symptomatic 50–99% stenosis, not asymptomatic disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 68-year-old smoker with calf claudication has spectral Doppler at the ankle showing a monophasic, low-velocity, damped waveform with a slow systolic upstroke. What does this indicate?
options: Distal small-vessel disease only, with normal proximal arteries
A significant stenosis or occlusion located proximal to the probe
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: A significant stenosis or occlusion located proximal to the probe
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Normal peripheral arteries are triphasic. Damping to a monophasic, low-velocity waveform reflects significant obstruction upstream; tracing the probe proximally until the waveform normalises brackets the culprit lesion.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: During duplex, the peak systolic velocity within a narrowed superficial femoral artery segment is more than twice that of the adjacent normal proximal segment. This velocity ratio >2:1 best corresponds to:
options: An imaging artefact requiring no action
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: A haemodynamically significant ≥50% stenosis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: A peak systolic velocity ratio >2:1 across a stenosis indicates a haemodynamically significant ≥50% diameter stenosis. Complete occlusion would instead show absent colour and spectral flow.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 60-year-old with long-standing diabetes and CKD has an ABPI of 1.4 but reports rest pain and has a non-healing toe ulcer. What is the most likely explanation for the ABPI value?
options: Truly excellent arterial perfusion, so ischaemia is excluded
Venous insufficiency causing the high index
Measurement error from an oversized cuff only
Falsely elevated ABPI from incompressible calcified vessels masking severe disease
Normal physiological variation needing no further assessment
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Falsely elevated ABPI from incompressible calcified vessels masking severe disease
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: ABPI >1.3 suggests incompressible, calcified vessels (common in diabetes and CKD), giving a falsely high index that can mask severe PAD. The clinical picture (rest pain, ulcer) points to critical limb ischaemia; assess waveforms/toe pressures and refer urgently.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 41-year-old woman has hypertension resistant to three agents and an epigastric bruit. Renal artery Doppler prompts angiography showing a mid-vessel 'string of beads' appearance. What is the most likely underlying cause?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Fibromuscular dysplasia
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: A young woman with resistant hypertension, an abdominal bruit and a mid-to-distal 'string of beads' pattern is the classic picture of fibromuscular dysplasia, which typically responds well to angioplasty. Atherosclerotic lesions are ostial and occur in older arteriopaths.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: Which Doppler finding is a recognised sign of haemodynamically significant renal artery stenosis?
options: Peak systolic velocity <50 cm/s at the origin
Reversed diastolic flow in the aorta
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Downstream intrarenal tardus-parvus waveform
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Significant stenosis produces a high-velocity jet at the narrowing (raised PSV >180–200 cm/s, renal-aortic ratio >3.5) and a dampened downstream 'tardus-parvus' waveform with a delayed slow systolic upstroke and low resistive index. A renal-aortic ratio of 1.2 and low PSV are normal.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 68-year-old man with bilateral renal artery stenosis is started on ramipril and his creatinine rises sharply over a week. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Continue ramipril and repeat creatinine in 3 months
Add a second antihypertensive to control BP
Arrange routine outpatient renal Doppler in 6 weeks
Stop the ACE inhibitor and seek urgent renal/vascular input
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Stop the ACE inhibitor and seek urgent renal/vascular input
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: In bilateral RAS (or RAS to a solitary kidney) glomerular filtration depends on efferent arteriolar tone maintained by angiotensin II. Blocking it with an ACEi/ARB drops filtration pressure and causes a sharp creatinine rise. The drug should be stopped and urgent specialist input sought.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: According to the randomised trial evidence, what is the role of stenting in atherosclerotic RAS?
options: Routine stenting clearly improves survival and should be offered to all
Routine stenting does not clearly improve outcomes over optimal medical therapy
Stenting is contraindicated in all forms of RAS
Stenting is first-line before any medical therapy is tried
Stenting reliably reverses established renal atrophy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Routine stenting does not clearly improve outcomes over optimal medical therapy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Trials of atherosclerotic RAS showed routine stenting added to medical therapy did not clearly improve blood pressure or renal outcomes. Revascularisation is reserved for selected cases such as FMD, flash pulmonary oedema or rapidly declining renal function.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: Which presentation should most strongly prompt consideration of renal artery stenosis?
options: Painless visible haematuria with weight loss
Recurrent 'flash' pulmonary oedema with resistant hypertension
Bilateral loin pain with fever and pyuria
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Recurrent 'flash' pulmonary oedema with resistant hypertension
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Recurrent sudden ('flash') pulmonary oedema without a cardiac cause, especially with resistant hypertension, is a recognised presentation of RAS (often bilateral) and should prompt renal artery Doppler. The other options point to glomerular, urological or infective pathology.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 58-year-old man with known alcohol-related cirrhosis has an abdominal Doppler ultrasound. Which finding would most specifically indicate portal hypertension?
options: Hepatopetal portal vein flow at 25 cm/s
A sharply pulsatile hepatic arterial waveform
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Reversed (hepatofugal) portal vein flow
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Reversal of portal flow away from the liver is the most specific Doppler sign of portal hypertension, reflecting decompression through collaterals. An 11 mm vein and 25 cm/s hepatopetal flow are normal; gallbladder wall thickening and a pulsatile hepatic artery are non-specific.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A patient with cirrhosis and a rising AFP is found to have echogenic material filling the main portal vein. Which Doppler feature would most strongly suggest tumour thrombus rather than bland thrombus?
options: Complete absence of any flow signal
Cavernous transformation of the portal vein
Arterial flow signal within the thrombus
Turbulent flow in the hepatic veins
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Arterial flow signal within the thrombus
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Bland thrombus is avascular. Neovascular arterial flow WITHIN the thrombus indicates tumour thrombus, which in a cirrhotic with rising AFP points to HCC invading the portal vein. Cavernous transformation indicates chronic bland occlusion; the other findings are non-specific.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A young woman with a myeloproliferative disorder presents with abdominal pain, tense ascites and deranged LFTs. Doppler shows absent hepatic vein flow and hepatic vein thrombosis. Which additional finding best supports the diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Caudate lobe hypertrophy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: This is Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic venous outflow obstruction). The caudate lobe hypertrophies because it drains separately, directly into the IVC, and is spared the outflow block. A dilated CBD, splenic vein aneurysm and normal portal diameter are unrelated to the diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A 64-year-old on haemodialysis has a 7-week-old radiocephalic fistula that is difficult to needle. Duplex shows access flow of 350 mL/min, vein diameter 4 mm and a focal 4-fold rise in peak systolic velocity just beyond the anastomosis. What is the most likely explanation for failure to mature?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Juxta-anastomotic stenosis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Low access flow (<600 mL/min), small vein (<6 mm) and a focal PSV ratio >2–3 just past the anastomosis indicate a juxta-anastomotic stenosis — the classic cause of poor maturation, warranting angioplasty. The other options do not produce a focal velocity step-up with low flow.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: During pre-operative vein mapping for AV fistula creation, which single ultrasound finding best predicts a suitable venous outflow target?
options: Presence of heavy arterial wall calcification
Vein depth greater than 8 mm from the skin
Cephalic vein diameter ≥2–2.5 mm, patent and distensible
Retrograde flow in the distal radial artery
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Cephalic vein diameter ≥2–2.5 mm, patent and distensible
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: A patent, distensible, superficial vein ≥2–2.5 mm is the target for outflow. A tiny radial artery and heavy calcification predict inflow failure, an overly deep vein is hard to cannulate, and distal retrograde radial flow suggests steal — none is a marker of a good outflow vein.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A dialysis patient presents with a fistula arm that has suddenly lost its thrill and bruit; duplex shows echogenic material filling the lumen with no detectable flow. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Urgent referral for thrombectomy/salvage to preserve access
Start oral antiplatelet therapy and discharge
Measure access volume flow and continue routine dialysis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: Urgent referral for thrombectomy/salvage to preserve access
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: Absent thrill/bruit with no Doppler flow and intraluminal clot indicates a thrombosed access — an emergency. Rapid thrombectomy or salvage preserves the dialysis lifeline; delay, antiplatelets alone, or elective ligation all risk permanent loss of the access.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.question: A patient with a swollen leg has a non-compressible popliteal vein on ultrasound. What is the first-line treatment?
options: A DOAC (e.g. apixaban) for at least 3 months
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.answer: A DOAC (e.g. apixaban) for at least 3 months
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Vascular / D.explanation: A non-compressible vein confirms a proximal DVT. First-line treatment is a DOAC (apixaban or rivaroxaban) for a minimum of 3 months; duration is extended for unprovoked or ongoing-risk DVT.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 68-year-old man with breathlessness has a TTE. Which single view is most reliable for detecting and assessing a pericardial effusion?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Subcostal view
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: The subcostal window images the heart from below the xiphisternum and is the most reliable single view for pericardial effusion and for assessing the IVC. It is also the standard tamponade/emergency view. The other windows can show effusions but the subcostal view is classically the best answer.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A hypotensive, breathless patient has a large pericardial effusion on echo. Which finding most strongly indicates cardiac tamponade requiring emergency pericardiocentesis?
options: Mild mitral regurgitation on colour Doppler
Diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis supported by echo. Rising intrapericardial pressure compresses the lower-pressure right-sided chambers, causing diastolic collapse of the RA and RV. Combined with hypotension and breathlessness this mandates urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis. The other findings are incidental and do not indicate tamponade.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which statement about the relative roles of transthoracic (TTE) and transoesophageal (TOE) echo is correct?
options: TTE uses ionising radiation and should be limited in young patients
TOE gives superior images when TTE windows are poor, such as in obesity or ventilated patients
TOE is the routine first-line test for breathlessness
TTE image quality is unaffected by body habitus or lung disease
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: TOE gives superior images when TTE windows are poor, such as in obesity or ventilated patients
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: TTE is the non-invasive first-line test but is operator-dependent and limited by poor windows in obesity, COPD and ventilation. TOE places the probe in the oesophagus directly behind the heart, giving superior images in these situations and for endocarditis, LA appendage thrombus and prosthetic valves. TTE uses no radiation and readily assesses regurgitation with colour Doppler.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: On TTE, a regional wall motion abnormality of the left ventricle most specifically suggests which of the following?
options: Ischaemic heart disease or prior myocardial infarction
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Ischaemic heart disease or prior myocardial infarction
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Regional (as opposed to global) wall motion abnormalities follow coronary artery territories and indicate ischaemia or infarcted/scarred myocardium from a previous MI. Global impairment is more typical of a dilated cardiomyopathy. The other options produce different echo signatures (effusion, valve gradients, shunt flow, elevated RV/PA pressures).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 68-year-old with persistent AF is booked for elective electrical cardioversion but has not had 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation. Which investigation is performed immediately before cardioversion to reduce embolic risk?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Transoesophageal echocardiography
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: TOE images the left atrial appendage — the usual site of thrombus in AF — which TTE cannot visualise adequately. Excluding appendage thrombus permits early cardioversion without the full 3-week anticoagulation window.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A patient with a prosthetic mitral valve and blood cultures positive for Staphylococcus aureus has a normal transthoracic echo. What is the most appropriate next imaging step to assess for endocarditis?
options: Repeat transthoracic echo in one week
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Transoesophageal echocardiography
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: TOE is far more sensitive than TTE for vegetations and valve abscess, and it overcomes the acoustic shadowing of prosthetic valves by imaging them from behind. A normal TTE does not exclude prosthetic-valve endocarditis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Before performing a TOE, which of the following is an absolute contraindication?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Known oesophageal varices
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Oesophageal stricture, varices, recent oesophageal surgery and an unstable cervical spine contraindicate TOE because passing the probe risks perforation or bleeding. AF, prosthetic valves and suspected appendage thrombus are in fact indications for the test.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 58-year-old with intermediate-risk stable chest pain has a dobutamine stress echo. At rest all segments contract normally; at peak stress the anteroseptal wall becomes akinetic and he reports chest tightness. What does this indicate?
options: Inducible ischaemia in the LAD territory
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Inducible ischaemia in the LAD territory
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: A segment normal at rest that becomes akinetic on stress is a positive test for inducible ischaemia. The anteroseptal territory is supplied by the LAD. A fixed abnormality present at rest and unchanged would suggest scar instead.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: During low-dose dobutamine echo of a patient with prior infarction and poor LV function, an akinetic segment improves contraction at low dose but deteriorates at higher dose. This biphasic response indicates:
options: Transmural scar with no recovery potential
Viable (hibernating) myocardium likely to recover after revascularisation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Viable (hibernating) myocardium likely to recover after revascularisation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: The biphasic response — improvement at low dose then worsening at high dose — is the classic marker of viable, hibernating myocardium. Identifying viability predicts functional recovery after revascularisation, unlike transmural scar which shows no contractile reserve.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which of the following is the strongest reason to STOP a stress echo and arrange urgent coronary angiography?
options: Development of chest pain with ST depression and a large new wall-motion abnormality
A mild rise in heart rate toward the target
Return of the LV cavity to its resting size
Mild breathlessness that resolves at rest
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Development of chest pain with ST depression and a large new wall-motion abnormality
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Provoked ischaemia with chest pain, ST changes, a large new wall-motion abnormality, or hypotension is a strongly positive test indicating significant flow-limiting disease. The test should be stopped, the patient treated, and urgent angiography arranged.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A patient has aortic stenosis with a low transvalvular gradient but reduced LV ejection fraction. Dobutamine stress echo increases flow, the gradient rises substantially and the calculated valve area stays small. This indicates:
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: True severe aortic stenosis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: In low-flow low-gradient AS, dobutamine augments flow. If the gradient rises and the valve area remains small, the stenosis is truly severe. If the valve area instead increases with flow, it is pseudo-severe (the low gradient reflected weak LV function).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 34-year-old woman presents with a cryptogenic ischaemic stroke and no vascular risk factors. During an agitated saline echo, a shower of bubbles appears in the left atrium within 3 beats of contrast reaching the right atrium, markedly increased on Valsalva release. What is the most likely finding?
options: Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunt
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Patent foramen ovale with right-to-left shunt
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Bubbles crossing to the left heart within ~3–5 beats, accentuated by Valsalva, indicate an intracardiac right-to-left shunt — most commonly a PFO. A pulmonary AVM causes delayed (>5 beat) opacification, and the other options do not shunt agitated saline into the left atrium.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: An echo technician performs a bubble study and sees the left atrium opacify only after about 6–8 cardiac cycles, with a diffuse rather than sharp appearance of bubbles. Which diagnosis does this pattern most suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Intrapulmonary shunt (e.g. pulmonary AVM)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Delayed left-heart opacification after ~5 beats, having passed through the lungs, indicates an intrapulmonary shunt such as a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation. Intracardiac shunts (PFO/ASD) opacify the left heart early, within 3–5 beats.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A ventilated, obese patient has a technically difficult echo with poorly seen endocardial borders, making ejection fraction assessment unreliable. Which agent and purpose is most appropriate?
options: Agitated saline to detect a right-to-left shunt
Iodinated contrast for a CT coronary angiogram
Commercial microbubble contrast to opacify the LV cavity
Agitated saline with Valsalva to unmask a PFO
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Commercial microbubble contrast to opacify the LV cavity
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Commercial microbubbles cross the pulmonary circulation to opacify the left ventricle, sharpening endocardial border definition and improving EF assessment (and detection of apical thrombus/HCM). Agitated saline stays in the right heart and does not opacify the LV; the imaging modality here is echo, not CT or MRI.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 60-year-old man is in PEA cardiac arrest. During the rhythm-check pause a clinician performs a subcostal FoCUS view showing a large circumferential pericardial effusion with a barely moving heart. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Continue CPR and perform urgent pericardiocentesis for tamponade
Stop CPR and arrange an urgent formal transthoracic echo for quantification
Give a fluid bolus and reassess the IVC
Administer thrombolysis for presumed pulmonary embolism
Prolong the pulse-check pause to obtain additional parasternal views
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Continue CPR and perform urgent pericardiocentesis for tamponade
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: The findings indicate cardiac tamponade, a reversible cause of arrest. Management is immediate pericardiocentesis while minimising interruptions to chest compressions. A formal TTE is inappropriate here — FoCUS answers the binary question and action must follow at once.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which statement best describes the appropriate scope of focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS)?
options: It provides a precise, measured ejection fraction to replace formal echo
It must be performed only by accredited cardiac sonographers
It is a qualitative, goal-directed scan answering specific binary questions and integrated with the clinical picture
It is used to obtain detailed valve gradients and diastolic function
It should be interpreted in isolation from the clinical context
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: It is a qualitative, goal-directed scan answering specific binary questions and integrated with the clinical picture
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: FoCUS is qualitative and rapid, performed by trained clinicians to answer focused binary questions, always interpreted with the clinical picture. Precise quantification, valve gradients and diastology are the remit of a formal TTE by an accredited sonographer.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A hypotensive, tachycardic patient with pleuritic chest pain and hypoxia undergoes FoCUS. The apical 4-chamber view shows a dilated right ventricle larger than the left ventricle with a D-shaped septum. Which diagnosis does this most strongly suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Massive pulmonary embolism
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Acute RV dilatation and strain (RV larger than LV, D-shaped septum from pressure/volume overload) in a shocked, hypoxic patient point to massive PE as an obstructive cause. This may prompt thrombolysis. Tamponade shows an effusion, and hypovolaemia shows a small hyperdynamic LV with a flat IVC.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 68-year-old with breathlessness has an echo showing EF 35% by Simpson's biplane. Which statement best classifies this finding?
options: EF is normal and excludes heart failure
This is HFpEF, driven by diastolic dysfunction
This is HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction)
EF cannot be interpreted without fractional shortening
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: This is HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: An EF of 35% is ≤40%, defining heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). HFmrEF is 41–49% and HFpEF requires EF ≥50%. A reduced EF reflects impaired systolic (contractile) function.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 74-year-old hypertensive woman has exertional dyspnoea, raised NT-proBNP and EF 58%. Echo shows E/e′ 18, an enlarged left atrium and LVH. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)
Normal age-related echo, no heart failure
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: EF ≥50% with symptoms/signs, raised natriuretic peptides and structural/functional abnormality (raised E/e′, LA enlargement, LVH) defines HFpEF. Elevated E/e′ (>14) indicates high LV filling pressures from a stiff, poorly relaxing ventricle.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which set of echo parameters is used specifically to assess diastolic (rather than systolic) LV function?
options: Mitral inflow E/A, tissue Doppler e′ and E/e′ ratio
Regional wall motion score and EF
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Mitral inflow E/A, tissue Doppler e′ and E/e′ ratio
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Diastolic function is assessed with mitral inflow pulsed Doppler (E and A waves, E/A ratio), tissue Doppler mitral annular e′, the E/e′ ratio, left atrial volume index and TR velocity. EF and fractional shortening measure systolic function.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: An 78-year-old man with exertional syncope has an echo showing a calcified aortic valve. CW Doppler records a peak velocity of 4.6 m/s. Using the modified Bernoulli equation, what is the approximate peak pressure gradient across the valve?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: 85 mmHg
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: ΔP = 4v² = 4 × (4.6)² = 4 × 21.16 ≈ 85 mmHg. This peak velocity (>4 m/s) and gradient indicate severe aortic stenosis, and exertional syncope makes this symptomatic severe AS requiring urgent valve intervention.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which echocardiographic finding best indicates SEVERE aortic regurgitation?
options: Holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta
A long pressure half-time on the regurgitant jet
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending aorta
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Holodiastolic (pan-diastolic) flow reversal in the descending/abdominal aorta is a marker of severe AR. Severe AR also produces a SHORT (not long) pressure half-time and a WIDE vena contracta. A peak velocity >4 m/s is a criterion for aortic stenosis, not regurgitation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis has echo assessment of valve severity. Which valve area indicates SEVERE mitral stenosis, and what leaflet appearance is characteristic?
options: <1.0 cm²; systolic anterior motion of the anterior leaflet
<1.5 cm²; "hockey-stick" diastolic doming of the anterior leaflet
<2.5 cm²; myxomatous prolapse of both leaflets
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: <1.5 cm²; "hockey-stick" diastolic doming of the anterior leaflet
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Severe mitral stenosis is a valve area <1.5 cm² (measured by planimetry or pressure half-time). The thickened anterior leaflet domes in diastole, giving the classic "hockey-stick" appearance. Systolic anterior motion relates to HOCM, and flail/myxomatous leaflets cause regurgitation rather than stenosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 58-year-old man is hypotensive and breathless 3 days after an anterior STEMI. Echo shows a small circumferential effusion with early-diastolic inward buckling of the right ventricular free wall and a dilated IVC that does not collapse. Which finding is the MOST SPECIFIC echo sign of tamponade here?
options: Exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral inflow
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Right ventricular diastolic collapse
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: RV diastolic collapse is the most specific echo sign of tamponade. RA collapse is the most sensitive/earliest; the plethoric IVC and inflow variation are supportive but less specific. Size alone does not diagnose tamponade.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: On a parasternal long-axis view you see an anechoic stripe. It tracks posterior to the descending thoracic aorta. What is the most likely explanation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Pleural effusion
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Fluid posterior to the descending aorta is pleural; pericardial fluid tracks anterior to the aorta. The fat pad is anterior and speckled, not a clear posterior stripe.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which patient scenario is MOST likely to produce tamponade at the smallest effusion volume?
options: Chronic uraemic pericardial effusion of 1.2 L
Malignant effusion accumulating over several weeks
Acute haemopericardium from post-MI free-wall rupture
Chronic idiopathic circumferential effusion of 800 mL
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Acute haemopericardium from post-MI free-wall rupture
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Speed of accumulation determines tamponade. A rapid bleed (free-wall rupture, trauma, dissection, post-procedure) can tamponade at ~150–200 mL because the non-compliant pericardium cannot stretch, whereas slowly accumulating large effusions are tolerated.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A shocked patient with a pericardial effusion is being managed while awaiting drainage. Which intervention should be AVOIDED?
options: Aggressive IV diuresis to reduce cardiac workload
Cautious IV fluid to support preload
Preparation for surgical drainage if loculated
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Aggressive IV diuresis to reduce cardiac workload
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: The tamponading heart is preload-dependent; over-diuresis lowers filling pressure and can precipitate cardiovascular collapse. Give fluids to support preload and arrange urgent drainage.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A patient in PEA cardiac arrest has point-of-care echo showing a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with a swinging heart. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Continue chest compressions and give repeated adrenaline only
Immediate pericardiocentesis / drainage of the effusion
Obtain a formal CT before any intervention
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Immediate pericardiocentesis / drainage of the effusion
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Tamponade is a reversible cause of PEA arrest. An effusion with a swinging heart in a peri-arrest patient warrants immediate drainage rather than delay for further imaging.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A 58-year-old woman receiving trastuzumab for HER2-positive breast cancer has a surveillance echo. Her ejection fraction is 58% (unchanged), but her GLS has fallen from −21% to −16% since baseline. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her, as the EF is preserved and normal
Stop all cardiac follow-up as GLS is unreliable
Refer to cardio-oncology for consideration of cardioprotection despite normal EF
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Refer to cardio-oncology for consideration of cardioprotection despite normal EF
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: The GLS has fallen by about 24% relative to baseline (−21% to −16%), a relative drop >15%. This signals subclinical cancer-therapy-related cardiac dysfunction even though EF is preserved. The point of serial GLS is to intervene with cardioprotection before EF falls, so referral is correct; reassurance would miss early, more reversible injury.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which statement about GLS values is correct?
options: A GLS of −12% represents better function than −20%
A normal GLS is approximately −18% to −20% or more negative
GLS is a positive number because muscle lengthens in systole
GLS of 0% indicates the healthiest myocardium
A less negative GLS reflects improved contraction
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: A normal GLS is approximately −18% to −20% or more negative
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: Strain is negative because myocardium shortens during systole; normal GLS is around −18% to −20% or more negative. 'More negative = better', so −20% is healthier than −12%. A less negative value reflects worse, not improved, function, and 0% would mean no shortening at all.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: A patient with heart failure and preserved EF has an echo showing a bull's-eye map with markedly reduced strain in the basal and mid segments but relatively preserved apical strain. Which diagnosis does this pattern most strongly suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: Cardiac amyloidosis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: The 'apical sparing' or 'cherry on top' pattern — reduced basal and mid strain with preserved apical strain on the GLS bull's-eye — is a classic and relatively specific sign of cardiac amyloidosis. It is one of the situations where GLS adds diagnostic value beyond EF.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.question: Which of the following is a genuine advantage of GLS over visually estimated ejection fraction?
options: It is angle-independent, more reproducible and less load-dependent
It is completely independent of the ultrasound vendor/software used
It requires no echocardiographic images to calculate
It can only be measured from the parasternal short-axis view
It rises (becomes more positive) as function worsens
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.answer: It is angle-independent, more reproducible and less load-dependent
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Echocardiogr.explanation: GLS is angle-independent, more reproducible and less load-dependent than eyeball EF, and detects subclinical dysfunction earlier. It is derived from the three apical views, still requires images, and is in fact vendor-dependent (a limitation). Worsening function makes GLS less negative, not more positive.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 42-year-old woman has a solitary thyroid nodule. Which single ultrasound feature is MOST suspicious of malignancy?
options: Purely cystic content with posterior enhancement
Punctate microcalcifications within a solid hypoechoic nodule
A thin, well-defined hypoechoic halo around the nodule
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Punctate microcalcifications within a solid hypoechoic nodule
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Microcalcifications represent psammoma bodies and are strongly associated with papillary carcinoma, especially in a solid hypoechoic nodule. Cystic/spongiform content, comet-tail artefact and a well-defined halo are reassuring benign features.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A thyroid nodule is reported as U4 on ultrasound. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as the nodule is benign
Start levothyroxine to suppress the nodule
Request a radionuclide uptake scan to assess function
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: U3–U5 nodules require US-guided FNA for cytological (Thy) assessment before any surgical decision. U4 is 'suspicious', so tissue sampling and MDT discussion — not reassurance, suppression or immediate surgery — is the correct next step. Radionuclide scanning assesses function, not malignant risk.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: Colour Doppler of a diffusely enlarged thyroid shows florid, widespread hypervascularity described as a 'thyroid inferno'. Which diagnosis does this suggest?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: The 'thyroid inferno' — diffuse, exuberant colour-Doppler signal in an enlarged gland — is characteristic of Graves' disease. Hashimoto's is typically heterogeneous, hypoechoic and micronodular; the malignancies present as focal masses rather than diffuse hypervascularity.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: Which statement about thyroid ultrasound is correct?
options: Ultrasound reliably identifies a 'hot' toxic nodule
A taller-than-wide nodule (AP > transverse) is a reassuring benign sign
Ultrasound is the investigation of choice to assess thyroid function
A rapidly enlarging hard mass with hoarseness warrants urgent referral
Retrosternal goitre extent is best assessed by ultrasound alone
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: A rapidly enlarging hard mass with hoarseness warrants urgent referral
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: A rapidly growing, hard fixed mass with hoarseness (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement) raises concern for anaplastic carcinoma or lymphoma and needs urgent referral. 'Hot' nodules and function are assessed by radionuclide scanning and TFTs respectively; taller-than-wide is suspicious, not benign; and retrosternal extent is better shown on CT.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 34-year-old presents with a tender neck lump after a sore throat. Ultrasound shows a 12 mm oval node with an axis ratio of 2.6, a clear echogenic central hilum and central hilar Doppler flow. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Metastatic squamous cell carcinoma requiring urgent FNA
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Oval shape (ratio >2), a preserved echogenic fatty hilum and central hilar vascularity are the classic reassuring features of a benign reactive node, fitting the post-infective history.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: Which single ultrasound finding is MOST suggestive that a cervical node is malignant rather than reactive?
options: Loss of the fatty hilum with peripheral/chaotic vascularity
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Loss of the fatty hilum with peripheral/chaotic vascularity
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Loss of the fatty hilum and peripheral (capsular) chaotic flow indicate abnormal architecture and neovascularity typical of metastatic/malignant nodes; the other options are benign features.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 40-year-old has multiple bilateral rounded, markedly hypoechoic ('pseudocystic') cervical nodes with a reticular pattern; some retain a hilar-type vascular signal. He reports night sweats and weight loss. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as reactive nodes
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: The appearances plus B-symptoms suggest lymphoma. Persisting hilar flow can falsely reassure, and FNA is usually insufficient to subtype lymphoma, so core or excision biopsy is required.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 15-year-old presents with sudden severe left testicular pain for 3 hours, nausea, and a high-riding testis. Scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler is available. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange the ultrasound and await the report before deciding
Immediate surgical scrotal exploration and bilateral fixation
Discharge with analgesia and outpatient urology follow-up
Trans-scrotal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Immediate surgical scrotal exploration and bilateral fixation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: The story is classic testicular torsion, a clinical diagnosis and surgical emergency with a ~6-hour salvage window. You must not delay exploration for imaging when the presentation is classic; exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy is correct.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 28-year-old man has a firm, painless left testicular lump. Ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass. Which management step is CONTRAINDICATED?
options: Staging CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
Trans-scrotal needle biopsy of the lesion
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Trans-scrotal needle biopsy of the lesion
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: A solid intratesticular mass is a germ cell tumour until proven otherwise. Correct pathway is urology referral, markers, staging CT and radical inguinal orchidectomy. A trans-scrotal biopsy is contraindicated because it risks tumour seeding and disrupts lymphatic drainage.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 22-year-old has 2 days of gradually worsening right scrotal pain and dysuria. Doppler shows an enlarged, hyperaemic epididymis and testis with INCREASED flow and a small reactive hydrocele. Most likely diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Increased colour Doppler flow with a hyperaemic epididymis/testis and reactive hydrocele is epididymo-orchitis, the main mimic of torsion. Torsion shows the opposite — reduced or absent flow — which is why Doppler is the decisive discriminator.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with a palpable, mobile breast lump. What is the most appropriate first-line imaging investigation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: In women under ~40 the breasts are denser, limiting mammographic sensitivity. Ultrasound is first-line, radiation-free, characterises the lesion, and can guide biopsy. Mammography is added in older women.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: Which set of ultrasound features is MOST suggestive of a malignant breast lesion?
options: Anechoic with a thin wall and posterior acoustic enhancement
Smooth thin capsule with gentle lobulation
Homogeneous hypoechoic mass that is freely mobile
Taller-than-wide, irregular spiculated margins with posterior acoustic shadowing
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Taller-than-wide, irregular spiculated margins with posterior acoustic shadowing
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Malignant lesions grow vertically (taller-than-wide, non-parallel), have irregular/spiculated margins and cause posterior acoustic shadowing. Oval, wider-than-tall, circumscribed features and anechoic thin-walled cysts are benign.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 48-year-old woman has an irregular, taller-than-wide hypoechoic mass with posterior shadowing on US, plus an axillary node with cortical thickening and loss of the fatty hilum. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and repeat US in one year
2-week-wait referral for triple assessment and US-guided core biopsy
MRI only, with no tissue sampling
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: 2-week-wait referral for triple assessment and US-guided core biopsy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: These are suspicious (U5) features with abnormal nodes — breast cancer until proven otherwise. Urgent 2-week-wait referral for triple assessment with US-guided core biopsy (± FNA of the node) is required. Any persistent suspicious lesion needs a tissue diagnosis.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 45-year-old presents with recurrent left submandibular pain and swelling that worsen at mealtimes. Ultrasound shows a bright echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing and a dilated proximal duct. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Mealtime pain/swelling with an echogenic shadowing focus and proximal ductal dilatation is the classic picture of a submandibular stone — the commonest site because of viscous mucinous secretions draining uphill.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 68-year-old male smoker has a cystic, well-defined parotid mass; the contralateral parotid contains a similar lesion. Which tumour is most likely?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Warthin's tumour is characteristically cystic, frequently bilateral, and occurs in older male smokers. Pleomorphic adenoma is commoner overall but is typically solid, unilateral and lobulated.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 60-year-old has a firm parotid mass with ill-defined margins, abnormal adjacent nodes, and a new facial nerve palsy. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent head & neck/ENT referral for US-guided biopsy and MRI
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Urgent head & neck/ENT referral for US-guided biopsy and MRI
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Facial nerve palsy with a parotid mass is malignant until proven otherwise. Infiltrative margins, abnormal nodes and rapid change are red flags mandating urgent referral, US-guided biopsy, and MRI for staging and deep-lobe/nerve assessment.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A 45-year-old man has a soft, mobile lump on his back. Ultrasound shows a well-defined, compressible, elongated mass lying parallel to the skin, hyperechoic to fat with thin internal striations and no significant vascularity. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent referral to a sarcoma MDT
Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: These are classic ultrasound features of a benign lipoma. When appearances are typical, no follow-up or intervention is required and the patient can be reassured. Sarcoma pathways are reserved for indeterminate or red-flag lumps.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: Which ultrasound/clinical feature of a soft-tissue lump is MOST concerning for a soft-tissue sarcoma?
options: A mass measuring 6 cm and lying deep to the fascia
A visible punctum in the overlying skin
A preserved central echogenic fatty hilum
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: A mass measuring 6 cm and lying deep to the fascia
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: Size >5 cm and location deep to the deep fascia are among the strongest predictors of malignancy. Compressible anechoic contents suggest a cyst/ganglion, a punctum suggests a sebaceous cyst, a fatty hilum indicates a lymph node, and posterior enhancement is typical of cystic lesions.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.question: A patient has a firm 7 cm mass on the thigh that has grown rapidly over two months. Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous mass deep to fascia with internal Doppler flow. What is the correct next step?
options: Excisional biopsy in the outpatient clinic
Reassurance and interval ultrasound in 6 months
Referral to a sarcoma centre for MRI and image-guided core biopsy
Simple marginal excision by the referring surgeon
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.answer: Referral to a sarcoma centre for MRI and image-guided core biopsy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Small Parts.explanation: This lump has multiple red flags (>5 cm, deep to fascia, rapidly enlarging, heterogeneous, internally vascular) and is a sarcoma until proven otherwise. It must be referred to a specialist sarcoma centre for MRI and core biopsy before any excision; an unplanned excision worsens outcomes.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 68-year-old presents with a painful weak shoulder. Shoulder ultrasound shows non-visualisation of the supraspinatus tendon, fluid tracking into the gap, and the deltoid muscle lying directly on a bare greater tuberosity. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: A defect spanning the whole tendon with retraction/non-visualisation, fluid in the gap and a "naked" greater tuberosity (deltoid sagging onto bone) is the classic picture of a full-thickness tear. A partial tear would be a focal defect not crossing the full width; the other options do not produce a tendon gap.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: Which single feature best explains why ultrasound is chosen as the FIRST-LINE test for suspected subacromial impingement?
options: Superior visualisation of the glenoid labrum
Better assessment of muscle fatty infiltration than MRI
Higher sensitivity for cervical referred pain
Ability to scan the tendons dynamically during active movement
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Ability to scan the tendons dynamically during active movement
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: Ultrasound's key advantage over MRI here is that it is dynamic: scanning during abduction reveals bunching of the cuff/bursa under the acromion (impingement). Labral, bony and fatty-infiltration/deep detail are actually MRI strengths, and referred pain is a clinical, not ultrasound, consideration.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 30-year-old rugby player has sudden shoulder weakness after a heavy fall, with a positive drop-arm test, and ultrasound confirms a large full-thickness supraspinatus tear. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge with simple analgesia
Prompt orthopaedic/surgical referral to consider early repair
Assume adhesive capsulitis and start a physiotherapy-only programme
Long-term opioids and review in one year
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Prompt orthopaedic/surgical referral to consider early repair
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: An acute large full-thickness tear in a young patient after trauma with true weakness/positive drop-arm is a red flag for prompt surgical referral, as early repair is considered before the tendon retracts and the muscle degenerates. Adhesive capsulitis causes global passive stiffness, not a traumatic tear, and would not explain these findings.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A sonographer scanning the Achilles tendon notes a hypoechoic region on the long-axis image. On angling the probe to make it perpendicular to the fibres, the region becomes uniformly bright and fibrillar. What is the correct interpretation?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: True pathology (tendinopathy, tear) persists regardless of probe angle. A hypoechoic area that resolves into normal fibrillar echotexture when the beam is made perpendicular is anisotropy — an artefact from a non-perpendicular beam, not disease. Recognising this prevents overcalling normal tendons as abnormal.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 45-year-old presents after a sudden 'pop' in the calf during tennis. On dynamic ultrasound of the Achilles tendon, the two tendon ends are seen to separate and fail to move together when the ankle is passively plantarflexed. Which finding does this confirm?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: Dynamic scanning is key: in a complete rupture the tendon ends separate and do not move together during movement, with a gap and retracted refractile ends. A partial tear retains some intact fibres bridging the defect, so the ends stay connected on movement.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 30-year-old has a hot, swollen, exquisitely tender finger tendon sheath with fever. Ultrasound shows fluid and thickening within the sheath with marked Doppler hyperaemia. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection into the sheath
Urgent aspiration for Gram stain and culture plus empirical antibiotics
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Urgent aspiration for Gram stain and culture plus empirical antibiotics
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: A hot, swollen, tender tendon or joint with fever raises infective tenosynovitis / septic arthritis — an emergency. It requires urgent aspiration (Gram stain and culture) and empirical antibiotics. Corticosteroid injection is contraindicated in possible infection, and management should not be delayed.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 68-year-old man presents with a hot, red, exquisitely tender, swollen knee and a fever. Bedside ultrasound shows a moderate effusion with internal echoes. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Start empirical IV antibiotics immediately and review in 24 hours
Arrange an outpatient MRI to characterise the effusion before intervening
Prescribe oral NSAIDs and colchicine for presumed gout
Reassure and discharge as the ultrasound shows only a simple effusion
Perform urgent joint aspiration, send fluid for Gram stain, culture, WCC and crystals, then start antibiotics
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Perform urgent joint aspiration, send fluid for Gram stain, culture, WCC and crystals, then start antibiotics
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: A hot, swollen, painful joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Fluid must be obtained for urgent Gram stain, culture, WCC and crystals BEFORE antibiotics, since antibiotics reduce culture yield. Septic arthritis is a joint-destroying emergency requiring prompt washout and IV antibiotics — not delayed imaging or empirical treatment without a sample.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: On ultrasound of a swollen joint you find hypoechoic tissue distending the recess that does NOT compress under probe pressure and shows marked power Doppler signal. What does this represent?
options: The double contour sign of gout
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: Non-compressible hypoechoic tissue with increased power Doppler flow is synovial hypertrophy with active inflammation (synovitis), typical of rheumatoid/inflammatory arthritis. An effusion, by contrast, is compressible and shows no internal Doppler flow. Power Doppler positivity is a recognised marker of active disease.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: Which ultrasound finding is characteristic of GOUT (urate crystal deposition) rather than pseudogout?
options: Hyperechoic deposits within the substance of the cartilage
A compressible anechoic collection in the recess
Absence of any Doppler signal in the synovium
The double contour sign — a hyperechoic line over the cartilage surface
Uniform thinning of the articular cartilage
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: The double contour sign — a hyperechoic line over the cartilage surface
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: In gout, urate is deposited ON the surface of the hyaline cartilage, producing the double contour sign — a hyperechoic line parallel to and above the bright bony cortex. In pseudogout (CPPD), the hyperechoic deposits lie WITHIN the cartilage substance (chondrocalcinosis), not on its surface.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: During an ultrasound-guided subacromial injection you use an in-plane approach. Which appearance confirms you are visualising the needle correctly?
options: A continuous bright line running along the long axis of the probe showing the whole shaft and tip
A single bright dot crossing the ultrasound beam
Loss of all needle echo with only tissue movement seen
Colour Doppler signal filling the bursa
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: A continuous bright line running along the long axis of the probe showing the whole shaft and tip
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: In-plane technique aligns the needle with the probe's long axis so the entire shaft and tip appear as one continuous bright line — the preferred method because tip position is always known. A single bright dot is the out-of-plane appearance.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A patient presents with a hot, swollen, painful knee. The most important step before any corticosteroid injection is to:
options: Inject corticosteroid plus local anaesthetic to settle the inflammation
Give hyaluronic acid to protect the cartilage
Aspirate the joint and send fluid for culture to exclude septic arthritis
Proceed with a blind injection to avoid delay
Arrange fluoroscopy to guide the needle
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Aspirate the joint and send fluid for culture to exclude septic arthritis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: Corticosteroid must never be injected into a potentially infected joint. A hot swollen joint may be septic arthritis — aspirate and culture first. Injecting steroid into an infected joint is catastrophic.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: Which of the following is a specific reason to inject around a tendon rather than into it under ultrasound guidance?
options: To reduce the cost of the procedure
Because tendons are anechoic and hard to see
To ensure the local anaesthetic works faster
Because intratendinous corticosteroid risks tendon rupture (e.g. Achilles)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Because intratendinous corticosteroid risks tendon rupture (e.g. Achilles)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: Corticosteroid injected directly into a tendon weakens it and can precipitate rupture, classically the Achilles. US allows you to confirm the injectate spreads around the tendon/within the sheath rather than into the tendon substance.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 62-year-old man has a clinically suspected but non-palpable right groin hernia. During ultrasound, a sac containing peristalsing bowel is seen bulging out on Valsalva, arising lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and tracking into the inguinal canal. What is the diagnosis?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: A sac arising LATERAL to the inferior epigastric vessels and passing through the deep ring into the canal defines an indirect inguinal hernia. A direct hernia would be medial to the vessels through the posterior wall; a femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a reducible groin lump that vanishes when she lies flat and refills on standing. Ultrasound shows a dilated structure at the sapheno-femoral junction with venous colour flow on Doppler. What is the lump?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: A saphena varix is a dilatation of the great saphenous vein at the sapheno-femoral junction. It classically collapses on lying flat, refills on standing/Valsalva, and demonstrates venous flow on Doppler — the key features that separate it from a hernia.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A 70-year-old woman attends A&E with a tender, irreducible lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Ultrasound shows a sac with a thickened bowel wall, no Doppler flow within that wall, surrounding free fluid, and dilated proximal bowel loops. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Urgent surgical referral for suspected strangulation
Reassure and arrange routine outpatient hernia repair
Attempt firm manual reduction in the department
Discharge with analgesia and safety-netting advice
Arrange an outpatient CT and review in two weeks
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Urgent surgical referral for suspected strangulation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: An irreducible, tender femoral hernia with absent Doppler flow in the bowel wall, free fluid, and obstructive features indicates strangulation with ischaemic bowel — a surgical emergency. Reduction should not be forced; urgent surgical referral is required. Femoral hernias strangulate more readily due to their narrow neck.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.question: A patient has a hot, swollen, painful knee with a joint effusion on ultrasound. The fluid looks anechoic. What is the priority?
options: Urgent joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals
Oral anti-inflammatories and review in 2 weeks
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.answer: Urgent joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals
investigations__ULTRASOUND__MSK.explanation: Anechoic fluid does NOT exclude septic arthritis. A hot joint needs urgent aspiration (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals) before antibiotics, plus orthopaedic involvement. Never inject steroid into a possibly septic joint.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a stabbing to the abdomen. He is tachycardic 130, BP 82/50, and not responding to fluids. FAST shows free fluid in Morison's pouch. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast to grade the injury
Admit for serial observation and repeat bloods
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Immediate laparotomy
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: A positive FAST in a haemodynamically unstable trauma patient indicates life-threatening haemorrhage and mandates immediate laparotomy. CT would dangerously delay definitive haemorrhage control; the patient is too unstable to leave the resuscitation area.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: Which of the following is the most dependent intraperitoneal recess in a supine trauma patient, making it the most sensitive FAST view for free fluid?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Morison's pouch (hepatorenal recess)
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: In the supine position, the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch) is the most dependent intraperitoneal space, so free fluid accumulates there first, making the RUQ view the most sensitive of the FAST windows.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A stable trauma patient has a completely negative FAST scan. Which statement is correct regarding interpretation?
options: A negative FAST reliably excludes all significant intra-abdominal injury
A negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal, hollow viscus, or small-volume bleeding
A negative FAST can be used to grade the severity of a splenic laceration
A negative FAST means CT is never indicated
A negative FAST excludes pericardial tamponade with certainty
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: A negative FAST does not exclude retroperitoneal, hollow viscus, or small-volume bleeding
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: FAST is insensitive to retroperitoneal bleeds, hollow viscus (bowel) injury, small-volume free fluid, and solid-organ injury without free fluid. If clinical suspicion persists despite a negative scan, CT or serial scanning/observation is required. FAST does not grade injury — that is CT's role.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A 24-year-old man is brought in after a stab wound to the left chest. He is tachypnoeic and hypoxic. Bedside lung ultrasound of the anterior left chest shows absent lung sliding, absent B-lines, and a barcode sign on M-mode. Scanning laterally you identify a point where sliding lung abruptly meets non-sliding lung. Which single finding confirms the diagnosis of pneumothorax?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: The lung point
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: The lung point — the transition between sliding and non-sliding lung — is pathognomonic for pneumothorax. Absent sliding and the barcode sign are supportive but not specific (they also occur with adhesions, mainstem intubation, ARDS and apnoea). The seashore sign is the normal M-mode pattern.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A 72-year-old woman presents with acute breathlessness and orthopnoea. Bedside lung ultrasound shows numerous vertical hyperechoic lines arising from the pleura, extending to the bottom of the screen, moving with lung sliding, and present bilaterally in multiple fields. What do these findings most likely represent?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: These are B-lines. Bilateral, diffuse B-lines (≥3 per field) indicate interstitial syndrome / "wet lung", most commonly cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (or ARDS). Pneumothorax abolishes B-lines; normal lung shows A-lines; effusion is an anechoic collection; pneumonia typically gives focal consolidation with hepatisation rather than diffuse bilateral B-lines.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A patient with previous trauma has absent lung sliding and a barcode sign on the left anterior chest. He is now hypotensive with distended neck veins and a trachea deviated to the right. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Arrange an urgent CT chest to confirm the diagnosis
Obtain an erect chest X-ray before intervening
Perform immediate needle or finger decompression
Continue scanning to locate a lung point first
Insert an intercostal drain only once bloods return
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Perform immediate needle or finger decompression
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: This is tension pneumothorax — a clinical diagnosis. With haemodynamic compromise, tracheal deviation and distended neck veins, treatment must not be delayed for imaging. Immediate needle or finger decompression is required, followed by a definitive chest drain. Searching for a lung point or awaiting CT/CXR wastes critical time.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A 68-year-old man presents with hypotension, muffled heart sounds and raised JVP. Subcostal POCUS shows a dilated IVC that does not collapse with respiration, plus a large pericardial effusion. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Give a rapid 2-litre crystalloid bolus to correct the hypotension
Start a noradrenaline infusion and observe
Commence systemic thrombolysis for presumed massive PE
Insert a chest drain for tension pneumothorax
Recognise likely cardiac tamponade and arrange urgent pericardiocentesis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Recognise likely cardiac tamponade and arrange urgent pericardiocentesis
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: A dilated, non-collapsing (plethoric) IVC with hypotension and a pericardial effusion is the classic POCUS picture of cardiac tamponade. The obstructed venous return means large fluid boluses will not fix the problem and may harm; definitive treatment is relieving the effusion. Thrombolysis and chest drain address different diagnoses not supported here (no RV strain or absent lung sliding described).

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: In a spontaneously breathing patient, which set of IVC findings best predicts that the patient is likely to be fluid-responsive?
options: IVC 1.0 cm, collapses more than 50% with inspiration
IVC 2.2 cm, plethoric, no respiratory variation
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: IVC 1.0 cm, collapses more than 50% with inspiration
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: A small IVC (<1–1.5 cm) that collapses more than 50% during spontaneous inspiration indicates low right atrial pressure and hypovolaemia, correlating with a higher likelihood of fluid responsiveness. Large, plethoric, poorly-collapsing IVCs indicate high RAP/venous congestion and warn against further fluid.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: Which statement about the limitations of IVC ultrasound is most accurate?
options: It reliably measures right atrial pressure in all mechanically ventilated patients
A dilated IVC in a young athlete always indicates fluid overload
The IVC diameter alone is sufficient to decide fluid therapy without other assessment
Respiratory collapsibility interpretation is confounded by high-pressure mechanical ventilation and raised intra-abdominal pressure
IVC assessment replaces cardiac and lung POCUS in the RUSH protocol
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Respiratory collapsibility interpretation is confounded by high-pressure mechanical ventilation and raised intra-abdominal pressure
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: IVC respiratory variation is confounded by high-pressure mechanical ventilation, raised intra-abdominal pressure, isolated RV failure and athletic physiology (athletes may have benignly dilated IVCs). It is a trend and adjunct, integrated with cardiac and lung POCUS within RUSH/FoCUS — never a standalone number to treat in isolation.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A 78-year-old man on the ward has passed no urine for 8 hours and is becoming confused. Before catheterising, a nurse performs a bladder scan showing an estimated volume of 30 mL. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The bladder is essentially empty, so this is not retention — investigate a pre-renal or renal cause of oliguria/anuria
He is in acute urinary retention and needs immediate catheterisation
The scan is unreliable and should be ignored in favour of immediate catheterisation
He has high-pressure chronic retention requiring urgent urology referral
The reading confirms normal bladder emptying and no further action is needed
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: The bladder is essentially empty, so this is not retention — investigate a pre-renal or renal cause of oliguria/anuria
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: An empty bladder in an anuric patient excludes retention. A catheter would add infection risk with no benefit; the problem lies with the kidneys or circulation, so assess volume status, perfusion and renal function instead.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: Which post-void residual volume is within the normal range for complete bladder emptying?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: 30 mL
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: A normal PVR is <50 mL. Up to ~100 mL may be acceptable in the elderly, but persistently raised residuals indicate incomplete emptying from outlet obstruction, neurogenic bladder or medications.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A bladder scanner reports 900 mL in a woman who has just fully voided and has no suprapubic discomfort. Real-time ultrasound shows a large adjacent cystic structure. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Genuine acute urinary retention despite recent voiding
A calibration fault making all readings invalid
Bilateral hydronephrosis being counted as bladder
The scanner has over-read because a large ovarian cyst was included in the measured field
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: The scanner has over-read because a large ovarian cyst was included in the measured field
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: Automated scanners can over-read when another fluid-filled structure — an ovarian cyst, ascites or a gravid uterus — lies in the field. An implausible volume should be confirmed with real-time imaging before acting.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: Which ultrasound finding most reliably identifies a vessel as a vein rather than an artery during central line insertion?
options: It collapses fully with gentle probe pressure
It shows a pulsatile waveform on Doppler
It is the smaller of the two vessels
It lies deepest in the scan field
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: It collapses fully with gentle probe pressure
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: Veins are thin-walled and compressible, collapsing with light probe pressure, whereas arteries are round, thick-walled, pulsatile and non-compressible. Compressibility is the key bedside discriminator, supported by colour/pulsed Doppler if doubt remains.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: According to NICE, what is the preferred technique for internal jugular central venous catheter insertion?
options: Palpation of the carotid pulse alone
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: 2D ultrasound guidance
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: NICE recommends 2D ultrasound as the first-line, preferred method for CVC insertion, particularly the internal jugular route, because it improves first-pass success and reduces complications such as arterial puncture and pneumothorax.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A large-bore catheter is discovered to have been placed in the carotid artery rather than the internal jugular vein. What is the correct management?
options: Leave the catheter in situ and seek urgent vascular/surgical advice
Immediately remove the catheter and apply firm compression for 10 minutes
Remove the catheter and observe for haematoma
Flush the catheter and re-site on the opposite side
Withdraw the catheter halfway and secure it
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Leave the catheter in situ and seek urgent vascular/surgical advice
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: Pulling out a large-bore arterial catheter and compressing risks catastrophic haemorrhage, stroke and airway compromise. It should be left in place while urgent vascular/surgical help is arranged. Confirming venous placement of the guidewire before dilating prevents this.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: In the short-axis (out-of-plane) approach to ultrasound-guided cannulation, how does the needle typically appear?
options: As the full length of the shaft within one plane
As a bright dot representing the needle tip crossing the beam
It is not visible at all
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: As a bright dot representing the needle tip crossing the beam
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: In short-axis the vessel is seen as a circle and the needle crosses the scan plane, so only a bright dot (the point where the needle intersects the beam) is seen. The operator must fan/track to ensure this dot is the true tip. Long-axis shows the whole shaft.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: Which complication is specifically reduced by using ultrasound guidance for internal jugular and subclavian central line insertion compared with the landmark technique?
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Pneumothorax
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: Real-time ultrasound reduces inadvertent arterial puncture, haematoma and — for IJ/subclavian access — pneumothorax, by allowing the operator to avoid the pleura and confirm the needle path. A post-procedure CXR or lung ultrasound still checks tip position and excludes pneumothorax.

investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.question: A 62-year-old man with obstructive uropathy has a fever, rigors and a raised WCC. Imaging shows a dilated, infected obstructed collecting system (pyonephrosis). He has been started on IV antibiotics but remains septic. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue antibiotics alone and reassess in 48 hours
Urgent decompression with a US/IR-guided nephrostomy for source control
Oral antibiotics and discharge with outpatient follow-up
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.answer: Urgent decompression with a US/IR-guided nephrostomy for source control
investigations__ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Car.explanation: An obstructed, infected system is an emergency. Antibiotics cannot sterilise an undrained obstructed pocket, so urgent drainage (nephrostomy) is required for source control alongside antibiotics. Nephrectomy is not the acute answer, and antibiotics alone risk ongoing sepsis.
